#676. A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived

A single ancient elephant tooth is offering scientists a remarkable glimpse into a world that existed nearly 700,000 years ago. Found in northern Israel, the fossil has helped researchers reconstruct a surprisingly lush prehistoric landscape filled with forests, rivers, wetlands, and abundant vegetation. This ancient environment supported enormous elephants and some of the region's earliest human populations, revealing how access to water and natural resources may have helped our ancestors survive and move between continents.

The discovery comes from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (GBY-NBA), an archaeological site where early humans produced stone tools hundreds of thousands of years ago. Elephant remains were unearthed alongside handaxes and cleavers made from basalt, a volcanic rock. These implements belong to the Acheulian tradition, one of the oldest and most widespread stone tool technologies in human history.

The research, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, was led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University). The team examined a large elephant molar and fragments of tusk recovered from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), situated in the Jordan Rift Valley just south of today's Hula Valley. The site was excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues.

A Giant Elephant Tooth Reveals a Lost Prehistoric World

The fossils belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, commonly known as the straight-tusked elephant. This enormous prehistoric animal was among the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene, the geological period that included the most recent ice ages.

Rather than focusing only on the animal itself, the scientists treated its tooth as a record of the world in which it lived. Teeth can preserve chemical clues about an animal's diet and surroundings, allowing researchers to investigate environmental conditions from hundreds of thousands of years ago.

To uncover those clues, the team combined several scientific techniques, including CT scans, 3D reconstruction, microscopic examination of tooth wear, isotope geochemistry, and pollen analysis. CT imaging allowed them to examine the fossil's internal structure, while chemical measurements and microscopic evidence helped build a picture of the ancient habitat.

The results pointed to a remarkably persistent landscape containing woodlands, open grasslands, marshes, flowing rivers, and shallow bodies of water. Carbon isotope measurements suggested that the elephant lived in an environment with a dependable water supply. Meanwhile, pollen preserved in nearby sediments revealed a variety of wetland plants, including reeds, sedges, willow, tamarisk, and aquatic vegetation.

Together, these findings suggest that the region offered a diverse and productive environment capable of supporting both giant mammals and early human communities.

An Ancient Oasis Along a Crucial Human Migration Route

The location of this prehistoric landscape makes the discovery particularly significant. The Hula Valley lies within the Levantine Corridor, a natural passage connecting Africa and Eurasia that played an important role in the movements of ancient humans and animals.

Researchers believe the area functioned as a relatively stable ecological refuge, maintaining vital habitats and resources over long periods. Its rivers, wetlands, forests, and grasslands would have offered dependable sources of water, vegetation, and animal life for populations traveling through the region.

For early humans, access to such environments could have made the difference between surviving in an unfamiliar landscape and being unable to sustain a population. Understanding these habitats may therefore help explain how ancient human groups moved through the region and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

According to Prof. Sharon, "understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species."

The findings highlight the importance of studying ancient landscapes alongside the fossils and artifacts found within them. By reconstructing the environments that supported prehistoric life, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the conditions that influenced early human survival and migration.

"The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive," Sharon says. "The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world's earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago."

The study brought together specialists from several Israeli universities. Farrell of the University of Haifa conducted the research using material from the site excavated by Sharon and his colleagues. Additional collaborators included Cheryl A. Makarewicz (isotope studies) and Nimrod Marom (archaeozoology) of the University of Haifa, as well as Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut (pollen studies) of Tel Aviv University.

Materials provided by Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#675. A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets

A star system just 16 light-years from Earth has puzzled astronomers for more than 170 years. Now, researchers have uncovered a surprising explanation for a signal that once suggested a giant planet was hiding there. Although the discovery rules out certain massive planets, it also helps narrow the search for smaller worlds that could potentially support life.

Led by the University of Michigan, the new study examined 70 Ophiuchi AB, also known as 70 Oph AB, a nearby binary star system in which two stars orbit each other. Using an exceptionally sensitive analysis, scientists searched for planets as massive as Jupiter or larger. Instead of finding one, they determined that such planets do not exist within the regions they examined.

That result might initially seem disappointing, but it represents an important advance. The researchers achieved the most sensitive modern search for giant planets in this particular system, using an approach that was not intended to detect smaller worlds. The work, supported in part by NASA, therefore leaves open the possibility that other planets remain undiscovered.

Among those possibilities are planets the size of Saturn or smaller, including rocky worlds that might exist within the system's habitable zone. This is the region around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to remain on a planet's surface, provided the planet has suitable atmospheric conditions. Because liquid water is essential to life as we know it, such worlds are especially interesting to astronomers searching for life beyond Earth.

The mystery surrounding 70 Oph AB began long before modern planet hunting. In 1855, British astronomer William Jacob proposed that the system contained a planet, making it the first star system to host an officially proposed exoplanet candidate. His claim was eventually rejected, but the possibility of undiscovered planets continued to intrigue astronomers for generations.

"It's a mix of disappointment and excitement," said Yiting Li, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We're finding out that there isn't a Jupiter-sized planet, but we're also opening the latest chapter on this historic system."

Unlike our solar system, which has only one star, roughly half of all stellar systems in the Milky Way contain at least two. These multiple star systems offer valuable opportunities to investigate how planets form, change over time, and potentially develop conditions suitable for life.

70 Oph AB is particularly attractive because of its proximity. Located approximately 16 light-years from Earth, it is the third closest binary star system to our planet, following Alpha Centauri (4.2 light-years) and 61 Cygni (11.4 light-years).

The new findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, also establish the orbits of the system's two stars, 70 Oph A and 70 Oph B, as some of the most precisely understood stellar orbits in the sky.

Future NASA Missions Could Search for Smaller Worlds

Knowing which planets are absent can be just as valuable as discovering new ones. By eliminating certain possibilities, the researchers have provided information that could make future searches more efficient and help astronomers focus on planets that remain within reach of upcoming observatories.

"The new limit enables us to design optimum search strategies in the future," said Michael Meyer, a senior co-author of the study and chair of the University of Michigan's astronomy department.

"In fact, the University of Michigan is part of a team studying a space mission called SHERA that will focus on binaries, where this system is one of a handful of targets. 70 Oph AB will certainly be a target of flagship missions, such as NASA's Habitable World Observatory."

Such missions could help scientists study smaller planets that current observations cannot yet detect or characterize. Rocky planets are especially important targets because they offer the possibility of environments similar to Earth, although finding one in a habitable zone would not by itself establish that life exists there.

Scientists Discover the True Source of a Mysterious Stellar Wobble

The research brought together scientists from more than a dozen institutions, including NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and IPAC at the California Institute of Technology.

Their analysis ruled out planets with masses equal to or greater than Jupiter's within specific parts of the system. Around 70 Oph A, no such planets were found within 5 astronomical units. Around 70 Oph B, they were excluded within half an astronomical unit. An astronomical unit is the average distance between Earth and the Sun, approximately 93 million miles.

These limits resolve a question that had persisted despite increasingly advanced observations. Although William Jacob's original claim from 1855 did not withstand later examination, measurements collected over the following 171 years had never completely eliminated the possibility of giant planets in the system's inner regions.

One particularly puzzling clue involved changes in the stars' radial velocity, which describes how quickly an object moves toward or away from Earth. Astronomers can use these changes to search for planets because an orbiting planet's gravity causes its host star to move slightly back and forth. This subtle motion produces a detectable "wobble" in measurements of the star's light.

For years, observations of 70 Oph AB revealed a wobble that could have been explained by a Jupiter-sized planet. The new research, however, points to a different cause.

To investigate, the team combined roughly a century of historical measurements with new observations from two major telescopes: the 6.5-meter Magellan Clay Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile and the 2.7-meter Harlan J. Smith Telescope at McDonald Observatory in Texas.

The resulting analysis was sensitive enough to distinguish the apparent planetary signal from changes occurring on the stars themselves. The researchers concluded that variations in stellar surface activity over time, rather than the gravitational influence of a giant planet, were responsible for the mysterious wobble.

"Yiting assembled an absolutely huge amount of data from all over the world and carefully explored all possibilities," Meyer said. "It's a cautionary tale about how stellar activity can mimic planet signals using the radial velocity."

The Search for Hidden Planets Is Far From Over

Despite ruling out giant planets in the surveyed regions, the findings do not mean 70 Oph AB is planet-free. Smaller planets could still orbit either star, and the system remains a promising destination for future observations.

The results illustrate an important challenge in the search for planets beyond our solar system. Stars are not perfectly stable objects, and changes in their activity can produce signals that resemble those created by orbiting planets. Separating these effects is essential for identifying genuine exoplanets, particularly smaller rocky worlds.

For 70 Oph AB, the latest discovery represents progress rather than a final answer. Scientists now have a clearer picture of what the system does not contain, along with better information for determining where to look next.

"The study sets an upper limit, not a ban, on planets," Li said. "Given how prevalent planets are in our universe and in the Milky Way, I would wager that we'll find there are other planets there."

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Heising-Simons Foundation.

#674. Pregnant SLOMW Star Jen Affleck Files for Divorce from Zac Affleck

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Jen Affleck, who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby, has filed for divorce after seven years of marriage.

Jen Affleck's marriage with Zac Affleck couldn't survive MomTok.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star—mom to kids Nora, 5, Luca, 3, and Penelope, 16 months, with a fourth baby on the way—filed for divorce from Zac on Nov. 3 after eight years together and seven years of marriage, according to Utah court records obtained by E! News.

E! News has reached out to Jen's rep for comment but hasn't heard back.

In recent years, Jen—who announced her pregnancy in June—and Zac's marriage troubles have been highly documented on Mormon Wivesand spinoff series The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, which saw the duo move to Southern California as they prepared to welcome another child.

Of course, with so many life changes comes plenty of relationship stressors, as Jen recently revealed.

"It’s been a lot the past couple of months, I’ll be honest," Jen confessed to People in August. "But I do feel like I’m seeing the light at the end of the tunnel and just trying to count my blessings every single day."

While Jen wasn't yet ready to say the "D" word at the time, she did admit, "There’s a lot that we’ve been navigating behind closed doors."

For starters, the 27-year-old struggled with prenatal depression during a rough first trimester.

"I could not be there for my kids, and so Zac really had to show up," she told the outlet, adding that though "he didn’t really have a choice," she also "wouldn’t have survived the first trimester" without the 29-year-old, whom she met in 2018 and wed one year later.

Not only that, but navigating life's ups and downs in the public eye comes with an added level of scrutiny.

While breakup rumors are nothing new for the exes, Jen previously shot down speculation their sometimes-contentious bickering on SLOMW was an indication they were headed for a divorce.

"It can be tiring and draining, just because it gets old having to hear the same things," Jen exclusively told E! in November 2025. "For me, I’m like, 'People will always talk and people will always have their opinions,' and I think it is frustrating for him when people don’t see what’s happening behind closed doors and how much work and effort he’s putting in."

Ultimately, Jen—who has shared her past struggles with mental health issues—focused on "tuning out the noise of the world" when she felt overwhelmed.

"It’s hard to have to constantly open your phone and see negative comments and it’s hard not to take that in," the social media star explained. "Even if you say you don’t take it in, subconsciously we all care to a certain point. For me, I always have to remind myself, I post, I share my story, and then I take a step back. #672. 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history

Deep within an ice cap in northwestern Tibet, scientists have uncovered evidence of a remarkable frozen record that may stretch back more than 128,000 years. The discovery suggests that ice high in the mountains has survived since the last ice age and could provide an extraordinary window into Earth's ancient climate.

The findings extend the known glacial record from the region by more than 100,000 years, making these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet. They also offer rare evidence of how mountain glaciers endured major changes in Earth's climate.

Researchers reached their conclusions by examining ice cores collected from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015. Despite being drilled 23 years apart, the samples revealed strikingly similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, which scientists use to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The close match indicates that the ice has preserved a reliable and reproducible record of climate history.

"Reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important," said Lonnie Thompson, lead author of the study, professor of earth sciences and senior research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center at The Ohio State University. "If you get an identical record a quarter of a century later, it can tell you a lot about the behavior of the ice over time."

How Scientists Dated the Ancient Tibetan Ice

Determining the age of ice that has remained frozen for tens of thousands of years is no simple task. To establish a more accurate timeline, the international research team turned to advanced dating methods involving radioactive isotopes of beryllium and chlorine.

These naturally occurring radioactive forms of elements decay at predictable rates, making them valuable tools for identifying events deep in Earth's environmental history. In this case, researchers used them to detect evidence of the Leschamp Geomagnetic Excursion, a dramatic disturbance in Earth's magnetic field that occurred more than 41,000 years ago and left distinctive chemical signatures in the ice.

The team then compared its findings with oxygen isotope records preserved in nearby Tibetan cave deposits. Together, the evidence suggests that the Guliya ice record may extend well beyond 128,000 years into the past.

"It's a really critical finding, because outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that go back that far," he said. "Records out of Huascarán only go back over 30,000 years, not over 100,000, so that makes Guliya a very unique record."

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

A Frozen Climate Record From the Last Ice Age

Ice cores are among scientists' most valuable sources of information about ancient climates. As snow accumulates and gradually becomes compressed into ice, it can preserve chemical clues about the atmosphere and environmental conditions at the time. By examining different layers, researchers can piece together how climate changed over thousands of years.

However, interpreting these records depends on knowing when each layer formed. Without a reliable timeline, even an exceptionally well-preserved ice core can be difficult to understand.

That uncertainty had complicated earlier interpretations of the Guliya ice cap. Previous research suggested that its record reached back only to the middle of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began nearly 12,000 years ago following the last ice age.

The new evidence establishes that at least some of the ice is considerably older than the Holocene. This also has important implications for understanding whether large ice masses in Tibet persisted as the planet emerged from the last glacial period.

"If we only had Holocene-era ice in Tibet, that would mean that the big ice sheets from the last ice age didn't persist through the early Holocene," said Thompson. "But evidence shows that it did."

What the Discovery Reveals About Earth's Glacial History

The Guliya ice cap's unusual geography may help explain why it has preserved such an exceptionally old climate record. Its high elevation and surrounding terrain likely contributed to conditions that allowed ancient ice to remain in place through major environmental changes.

Beyond establishing the ice's age, researchers hope that a more precise timeline will help answer fundamental questions about the history of Earth's glaciers. Knowing when major periods of glaciation began, how long they lasted, and when the ice retreated is essential for reconstructing the planet's natural climate cycles.

"When did ice start forming on the planet and what did those natural processes of loss look like?" said Thompson. "We need to know those things, and the only way you can really demonstrate it is with accurate time scales on these records."

The revised timeline also creates new opportunities to investigate the Guliya ice cores in greater detail. Researchers plan to study additional samples to determine how other indicators of past climate and environmental conditions fit into this much longer history.

Those future analyses could reveal information that was previously overlooked or interpreted differently because scientists did not fully understand the age of the ice.

For Thompson, one of the most encouraging aspects of the discovery is how consistently the different measurements support the same interpretation.

"The big picture is that our results tell a very consistent story," he said. "If you get the science right, it's consistent. It's our understanding of what it's trying to tell us that has to catch up."

The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Ohio State co-authors include Mary Davis and Ellen Mosley-Thompson. Other contributors were Juerg Beer of the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology; Christof Vockenhuber and Marcus Christl of ETH Zurich in Switzerland; Tandong Yao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; and Ninglian Wang and Ling Fang of Northwest University in China.

Swift is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 2:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 4: NASA's Swift space telescope fell to Earth today at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) over Indonesia. Read our story here.

NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will reenter Earth's atmosphere in an uncontrolled fashion, after a robotic rescue mission failed to boost the scope to a higher orbit.

Swift launched to Earth orbit back in November 2004. Over the next two decades, it studied gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe — and other cosmic objects and events using a trio of telescopes: a Burst Alert Telescope (BAT), an X-Ray Telescope (XRT), and its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT).

On Oct. 20, NASA reported that Swift's orbit had decayed to 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth and that the roughly 3,300-pound (1,500-kilogram) observatory was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag. It entered safe mode, followed by Swift's operations team at Pennsylvania State University sending a command to the spacecraft that effectively ended its operations ahead of its destructive and fiery nose-dive.

It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where Swift will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.

In physics fashion, for the most part, what goes up must come down — with more space hardware to follow.

Thanks to the growing surge in low Earth orbit constellations and technology refresh cycles, there are 10 times more objects reentering per year than there were just five years ago, said Darren McKnight, a senior technical fellow at LeoLabs, a company that keeps a watchful eye on what's going on above our planet.

"It is unfortunate that Swift was not 'reorbited,' but from a reentry hazard perspective it is a small portion of the stuff coming back in. The rub on this, of course, is that, while many people bemoan the reentry of more objects, I am much more upset about the rapid rate of abandoning massive objects above 400 miles [644 km]," McKnight told Space.com.

Swift will likely disintegrate sufficiently upon reentry to not pose a ground casualty hazard, McKnight said. However, the internal workings of the observatory's X-ray and optical telescope might survive, McKnight said.

Similar in view is Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at the U.K. precision-components supplier Accu Components.

"Once Swift falls to about 120 kilometers [75 miles], the end usually comes within a few minutes. The air in front of it heats up so much that the satellite will start to glow. Solar panels and antennas are typically the first to tear off, and at around 78 kilometers [48 miles], roughly eight times the height of a passing airliner, the main body breaks apart. Most of it will melt and vaporize," said Sladen.

While it isn't yet known exactly where any surviving pieces will land, Sladen noted that Swift's orbit only passes over a band within about 21 degrees of the equator.

"That band is mostly ocean, though it also crosses populated parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia and Latin America," he said.

As for which parts are most likely to survive and reach ocean or ground, Sladen pointed out that most of Swift's body is aluminum, wiring and electronics, which melt away early in the reentry process. What reaches Earth is usually small, dense and heat-resistant, such as titanium, steel and glass.

"The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors. Its mask of around 52,000 tiny lead tiles will almost certainly melt. Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down — nothing recognizable as a telescope," Sladen said.

Sladen said that, at the current time, it appears that no detailed risk assessment has been published for Swift's fall.

"However, this does not mean NASA has not done the work," said Sladen.

"NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published," he told Space.com. "Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork."

Sladen added that there's far more focus on how a satellite's life ends these days than there was in the past.

"Many now carry enough propulsion to steer themselves into a remote stretch of ocean, or are built from materials designed to burn up completely, an approach called 'design for demise.' NASA and the European Space Agency limit the chance of anyone being hurt by a reentry to one in 10,000, and if a satellite can't meet that, it's expected to come down in a controlled way," said Sladen.

So, should people be worried about having a nasty run-in with Swift leftovers?

Sladen doesn't think so. NASA has said that harm to anyone on the ground is unlikely, and LeoLabs also describes the risk as very small. Most of the spacecraft will burn up, and any surviving pieces will most likely fall into the sea, he said.

"The real concern is the long-term trend. With more satellites being launched than ever, the number of uncontrolled reentries is growing, which is why designing satellites to come down safely matters more and more," Sladen concluded.

On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet.

While it did end up flying by Mars, the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars.

When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars.

Ever since Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope to the red-tinted star and identified as a planet, Mars has captivated scientists' interests as to its nature. So it was of no surprise that as soon as we gained the ability to send missions into space, that the focus turned to the "fourth rock from the Sun."

As it turned out, though, reaching Mars, let alone entering its orbit or landing on its surface,, was and continues to be difficult.

Mars 1, despite its name, was actually the Soviet Union's fourth attempt at sending a probe to the planet. The first three ended in launch failures. Similar problems faced the United States, as well, but it was NASA's Mariner IV mission that became the first to successfully fly by Mars two years later.

Still, as humanity continues to push forward to the day people land on, explore and live on Mars, the 1962 Soviet mission stands as the first to get close to revealing the first details about the planet.

#668. NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s

NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.

Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.

Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.

How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind

The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.

At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.

Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.

Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System

Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.

The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.

Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.

"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."

The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.

Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.

Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.

"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.

Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.

What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars

Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.

Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.

These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.

"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.

Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.

NASA's Juno Makes Unprecedented Measurements

The breakthrough was made possible by observations Juno collected in December 2024. The NASA spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since July 2016, providing researchers with an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the giant planet and its surrounding environment.

A key part of the discovery came from the Juno Waves instrument, which was designed and built by physicists at the University of Iowa. The instrument measures electric and magnetic wave activity, allowing scientists to study the behavior of plasma around Jupiter.

Earlier spacecraft had detected the presence of bow shocks at outer planets, but they lacked the measurements needed to reveal the detailed structure of the plasma waves involved. Juno's observations have now provided a much clearer picture of how these waves behave at Jupiter.

The findings were published online on July 31 in Nature Communications in a study titled "Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock."

Additional contributors from the University of Iowa included Allison Jaynes, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, along with Jeremy Faden and Chris Piker, who provide research support in the same department.

The international research team also included Lynn Wilson III of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; John Connerney of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the Space Research Corporation; Frederic Allegrini of the Southwest Research Institute and the University of Texas-San Antonio; Rob Wilson of the University of Colorado-Boulder; Ali Sulaiman of the University of Minnesota; Scott Boltion and Robert Ebert of the Southwest Research Institute; and Barry Mauk of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#667. Influencer Liam Fitzgerald's Cause of Death Revealed

Liam Fitzgerald's cause of death was determined to be blunt force after he sustained injuries from an Oct. 30 motorcycle accident.

Officials have determined Liam Fitzgerald's cause of death.

The fitness influencer died from blunt force injuries sustained in an Oct. 30 motorcycle crash, with his manner of death ruled as an accident, a spokesperson for Broward County’s Office of Medical Examiner and Trauma Services told People Nov. 4.

Fitzgerald's girlfriend Jamie Lyn Rinaldi previously confirmed his passing, sharing that the 29-year-old "suffered severe injuries" in the crash.

"Despite the efforts of those who tried desperately to save him, they were unable to bring him back,” Rinaldi wrote on Instagram on Oct. 31. “There are no words to describe the heartbreak of this loss.”

It was a sentiment shared by his family, who remembered Fitzgerald as a "shining light."

“He had a way of lighting up every room he walked into, a personality impossible to forget, and a heart that loved deeply,” they shared in a Nov. 1 statement posted on his Instagram. “From family and friends to teammates, strangers, and people around the world, he inspired so many. He loved his people fiercely and would protect them with everything he had.”

"Liam’s work ethic was incredible," his family added. "When he put his mind to something, he gave it everything. He was talented at just about anything he tried and so proud of the life he was building and everything he accomplished."

Though his loved ones said Fitzgerald "had his own struggles, too,” they noted the content creator's aim was always to show "that no matter how hard life gets, you can always get back up and become a better version of yourself."

"He wasn't perfect, and never pretended to be. But he always strived to grow and do better," Fitzgerald's family continued. "His laughter, energy, accomplishments, and the memories he created will live on through everyone he touched."

They added, "Liam, you were one of a kind. You shined so bright, and the world is dimmer without you here."

#666. Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy

Mathematicians are raising a major challenge to one of modern cosmology's most widely accepted explanations: the idea that dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A presents mathematical findings that researchers at the University of California, Davis, say reveal a fundamental instability in the standard model of the expanding universe. Their calculations suggest that cosmic acceleration could emerge naturally from Einstein's equations, potentially eliminating the need to invoke mysterious dark energy.

The work challenges the Lambda-cold dark matter model, the leading framework scientists use to describe the universe's evolution since the Big Bang. The researchers reached their conclusions by studying the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein's theory of general relativity with equations describing how fluids behave. Together, these mathematical tools help scientists investigate everything from galaxies and black holes to the expansion of the cosmos.

A Hidden Instability in Our Model of the Universe

To explain the problem, Blake Temple, the study's corresponding author and a distinguished professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip.

"All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a 'solution of the equations,'" he said. "But it's unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away."

According to Temple, the team's mathematical analysis shows that Friedmann spacetimes, which form the foundation of conventional models of cosmic expansion, are unstable at both small and large scales in the context of the Big Bang. He described the standard solution as exceptionally unstable.

"Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical," Temple said. "You'll never observe them in nature."

This instability could have far-reaching consequences. If the universe naturally evolves away from the behavior predicted by these conventional models, its accelerating expansion might not require a separate form of energy to explain it. Instead, Temple argues, the answer could already be contained within Einstein's original theory of gravity.

"The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.

Why Scientists Believe Dark Energy Is Expanding the Universe

For nearly three decades, dark energy has been the leading explanation for one of astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the universe is not simply expanding, but its expansion is accelerating.

The concept has roots in Einstein's groundbreaking 1915 theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of space and time. Einstein originally believed the universe was static, neither expanding nor contracting. To make his equations compatible with that assumption, he introduced a mathematical term that counteracted gravity, calling it the "cosmological constant."

That assumption changed after Edwin Hubble discovered evidence in 1929 that the universe was expanding. Einstein famously referred to his introduction of the cosmological constant as his "biggest blunder," since his original equations without the additional term could have predicted an expanding universe.

The cosmological constant returned to prominence in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered that cosmic expansion was speeding up. It became closely associated with dark energy, the name given to the unknown component thought to be responsible for this acceleration.

Today's standard cosmological framework builds on the Friedmann universe, a mathematical description in which space expands while matter remains evenly distributed across the cosmos at any given moment. This assumption of large-scale uniformity plays a central role in how scientists reconstruct the universe's history.

But Temple and his collaborators began questioning whether the underlying mathematics could remain stable, prompting them to investigate other possible explanations for the observed acceleration.

Could Einstein's Equations Explain Cosmic Acceleration?

The researchers initially considered whether a massive shockwave might help explain the universe's expansion and the unexpected acceleration associated with it.

"Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave," Temple said. "Then we realized there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave."

In mathematics and physics, self-similar solutions describe patterns that retain their underlying structure when viewed at different scales. A familiar example is a fractal, in which similar shapes can appear at increasingly larger or smaller sizes.

The researchers identified a family of these solutions associated with the radiation-dominated period of the early universe, when radiation played a major role in determining how the cosmos evolved.

Building on their earlier work, they used a self-similar form of Einstein's equations to represent the standard cosmological model as a rest point, a mathematical state in which the system's defining variables remain unchanged. This approach allowed them to examine whether small departures from that state would disappear or grow over time.

Their analysis provided a mathematical framework for evaluating the stability of the standard model and, more broadly, Friedmann spacetimes during the matter-dominated era of the early universe, when matter became more influential than radiation.

A Mathematical Challenge to the Standard Big Bang Model

The results suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade.

"We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales," Temple said. "This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy."

Radial perturbations are disturbances that change with distance from a central point. In the researchers' mathematical framework, such changes can cause the behavior of an expanding universe to depart from the predictions of the standard Friedmann model.

"This means," he added, "that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the center of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the center."

In other words, the universe could behave much like the standard model predicts near a central region while exhibiting different expansion behavior farther away.

The researchers argue that this instability may offer a natural route to accelerated cosmic expansion without adding a cosmological constant or invoking dark energy. Their calculations indicate that the acceleration can emerge directly from the Einstein-Euler equations themselves.

The findings represent a theoretical challenge to standard cosmology rather than observational proof that dark energy is unnecessary. Establishing whether this alternative can describe the actual universe would require determining how well its predictions match astronomical observations.

Does the Universe Have a Special Location?

Beyond the dark energy question, the study also raises a more fundamental issue involving the Copernican principle.

Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who helped overturn the belief that Earth sits at the center of the solar system, the principle holds that our location in the universe is not fundamentally special or privileged.

This assumption has become an important part of modern cosmology, supporting the view that the universe looks broadly similar when observed from different locations on sufficiently large scales.

The researchers' alternative mathematical framework introduces a center of spherical symmetry, raising questions about where an observer would need to be located for the model to agree with observations.

Temple argues that the Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe.

"Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible," Temple said. "If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other."

The work opens another avenue for investigating why the universe's expansion is accelerating. Although dark energy remains a central component of the prevailing cosmological model, the researchers contend that the mathematics of general relativity may offer a different explanation for the same phenomenon.

If further theoretical and observational work supports their interpretation, it could lead to a significant reassessment of how scientists understand cosmic expansion and the mathematical foundations of the Big Bang.

The research received funding from the United Kingdom's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.

"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth. It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina.

That April 1 event — an incoming meteor, also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors.

Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic.

That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

This skyfall show is among a number of recent episodes that spotlight the value of combining multi-sensor data to not only portray fireball dynamics but also to help appreciate human-caused space debris impacts, as well as strengthening planetary defense knowhow.

Take, for instance, another extraterrestrial incident.

In this case, an April 24, 2025 fireball over south-central Alaska yielded one of the most densely recorded "seismoacoustic" datasets ever obtained for a nature-made bolide en route to busting up.

A network of 37 seismic stations, 16 single infrasound sensors, and four infrasound arrays recorded 30 ballistic and multiple fragmentation arrivals. All this was complemented by Doppler weather radar detections of falling meteorites and independent optical video observations.

Now, toss in for good measure yet another encounter.

A roughly 12-foot-wide (3.7 meters) space rock plowed through Earth's atmosphere over northwest Queensland, Australia, on May 20, 2023, accompanied by a raucous round of sonic booms. And U.S. government space-based sensors caught the fall.

Researchers later determined that the object underwent catastrophic fragmentation, producing one of the 20 most energetic events reported by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) since 1988 and the most energetic seen over Australia. It was equivalent to the explosion of a 7.1-kiloton bomb.

"For many fireballs, U.S. Government detections reported through NASA's CNEOS database provide an important starting point by establishing that an event occurred and, in many cases, providing basic parameters such as location, time and estimated energy," explained Elizabeth Silber, a senior research and development physicist at the U.S. Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico.

"Civil and scientific observing systems can then add independent measurements that help refine and validate that initial characterization," said Silber.

CNEOS, which is based at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, is NASA's center for computing asteroid and comet orbits and their odds of striking Earth. CNEOS computes high-precision orbits for such objects in support of NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office.

"The Alaska event is an especially useful example, because it was not reported by U.S. Government sensors in the CNEOS database. In this case, the event was reconstructed almost entirely from civil and scientific observations," Silber told Space.com.

She said that the seismic and infrasound data constrained the trajectory and acoustic energy, the video provided independent optical information, and the weather radar detected material from the fireball falling to Earth.

"So, the real strength is that these systems provide different and complementary information," said Silber. "When a U.S. Government detection is available, civil data can independently validate it and add much more detail. When one is not available, as in this case [for Alaska], the civil networks can still provide a surprisingly complete reconstruction."

The Alaska study shows how valuable it is to put together diverse types of observations once an event has occurred, said Silber. Each measurement responds to a different part of the event.

"Seismic and infrasound sensors record the atmospheric shock waves and can constrain the trajectory, fragmentation and energy," she added. "Optical observations provide an independent view of the luminous flight. Doppler weather radar can detect surviving material after it has slowed and entered dark flight."

Bottom line: no single sensor tells you everything.

"Combining independent observations lets us move from simply knowing that an event occurred to determining how the object traveled through the atmosphere, where it fragmented, how much energy it released, and whether material may have survived to the ground," said Silber.

Researchers got pretty lucky with the April 1, 2026 event over the South Atlantic, according to NASA's Rob Landis, a planetary defense specialist: Two civilian spacecraft located at different locations in geosynchronous orbit allowed them to conduct a rather unique investigation of this bolide.

"With two civilian resources, we can actually discuss things more openly," Landis, who's now a visiting vehicle integration manager for the International Space Station at NASA's Johnson Space Center, told Space.com.

Lightning-watching instruments not designed for detecting bolides, he said, "afford the science community to discuss these events and these sensors in a forthright, open manner. These lightning imagers give us opportunistic bonus science for those who study the 'hard rain.'"

Landis said that, in his personal view, there's a lot of smaller stuff getting through the atmosphere.

"To the casual observer, these certainly produce wonderful natural fireworks and are mostly harmless," Landis said. But, he stressed, it's important to be able to distinguish between natural events and human-made ones.

"It would be a horrific tragedy if any nation responded to a natural event — if they misinterpret it as a preemptive strike," cautioned Landis.

So, in the big picture, having collaborative, multiple and independent ways to observe atmospheric entries is of benefit to planetary defense thinkers.

"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth," Silber said. "It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry — that is, how the object fragments, where it deposits its energy, how accurately we can reconstruct its trajectory and whether material survives to the ground."

Incoming events provide "real-world tests" of the methods and models used to answer those questions, said Silber.

Harkening back to the recent Alaska fireball fall, Silber said, was particularly valuable because it was unpredicted, yet the dense ground-based network allowed the trajectory and energetics to be reconstructed in considerable detail.

"From a planetary-defense perspective, that kind of redundancy is extremely useful. Space-based observations, seismic and infrasound networks, optical cameras, and weather radar each provide different information, and each has its own limitations," Silber said.

When several observation techniques are available, researchers can cross-check one another and produce a much more complete characterization of an event.

"That improves post-event situational awareness, helps validate physical models and strengthens our ability to interpret future atmospheric entries, whether they involve natural objects or artificial reentries," Silber concluded.

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. #663. Allison Williams and Dad Brian Williams Have Rare Public Outing

Allison Williams and her dad Brian Williams made a rare joint appearance together, enjoying a father-daughter outing at a Falsettos anniversary concert in New York City on Nov. 2.

This just in: Allison Williams and Brian Williams are getting out on the town.

The Girls actress and former NBC News anchor shared a rare joint outing together to attend the Falsettos revival 10-year anniversary concert in New York City on Nov. 2.

For the outing at Carnegie Hall, Allison, 38, and Brian, 67, were all smiles as they posed for photos together.

The Get Out actress—who shares son Arlo, 4, with husband Alexander Dreymon—donned a casual, yet chic ensemble, wearing a black turtleneck with jeans, while accessorizing her look with a brown belt, glasses and colorful beaded bracelets.

As for Brian—dad to Allison with wife Jane Gillan Stoddard—the former news anchor sported a mustard yellow jacket over a button-up, matching his daughter with light-washed denim jeans.

But Allison didn’t just spend some quality time with her dad during the musical.

After all, the M3GAN star also hung out with her Girls costar Lena Dunham, who smiled for the camera alongside Allison and her dad.

And though Allison shares a strong bond with her dad, she didn't follow his footsteps into journalism. Still, she has acknowledged that she had a leg up in life thanks to her dad’s fame, describing her privilege as “thorough.”

"There's no conversation about my career,” she told Wired in 2022, “without talking about the ways in which I have been fortunate.”

“I was definitely concerned with making sure people understood I was a hard worker,” she continued, “as if somehow that would absolve me of the privilege.”

While she’s aware of how her upbringing may have looked differently than others, the Regretting You actress only looks back on it fondly.

“We had the best childhood,” Allison told her dad while appearing on his Netflix series We’re Back! With Brian Williams in June. “You were extraordinarily busy when I was growing up, and yet none of the sense memory I have of childhood is you not being there, which is really impressive because you had work hours that meant you weren't there for dinner.”

Ultimately, the Fellow Travelers actress feels “lucky” for how she and her brother Doug Williams were raised.

“When the topic of nepo babies and privilege comes up, I always start there,” she explained. “I always start at the fact that I felt totally loved and secure in my family unit growing up, and how that just sets you up on a totally different path in life.”

As Allison put it, “I felt like I had cheat codes in a way

To see what more stars had to say about the nepotism conversation, keep reading…

As the daughter of director J.J. Abrams and producer Katie McGrath, the "Close to You" singer believes "the nepo stuff is obviously in the discourse appropriately" when it comes to her career.

"I had a safety net and that allowed me the ability to experiment and to concentrate and I had the gift of time to dedicate to doing this thing I loved," she explained in a 2026 interview with the New York Times' Popcast. "I wasn’t growing up afraid financially and that’s the biggest deal."

Gracie continued, "And then the specific household that I was born into, there is just this vocabulary that I’m so lucky to grow up with. So like, when I see people pointing that out, it’s like, I get it hardcore."

"When that first started, I found it to be incredibly annoying and boring," the daughter of Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson said on the Feb. 7, 2024 episode of Today about the "Nepo Baby" debate.

Calling the issue "lame," the Fifty Shades of Grey star added, "So the opportunity to make fun of it, I jumped at"—referring to an SNL sketch poking fun at the controversy that she took part the previous month while hosting the show.

A reminder that this conversation has been going on for awhile, Emma was early in pushing back against the notion that being Julia Roberts' niece (and Eric Roberts' daughter) was the key to her career.

"A lot of people think that," the Scream 4 actress, then 20, told PopEater in 2011, "and they talk about nepotism which I think is so ridiculous considering it's obviously not true—because I've auditioned for so many things and never gotten the part. Also it's like, you know, maybe someone can get you one part, but they can't really get you 10 parts."

Goldie Hawn's daughter doesn't bother to get the knives out when talk turns to nepotism.

"I don't really care," Kate, who was also raised by Goldie's longtime partner Kurt Russell, told The Independent in December 2022. “I look at my kids and we're a storytelling family. It’s definitely in our blood. People can call it whatever they want, but it’s not going to change it."

The mom to sons Ryder and Bingham (with Chris Robinson and Matthew Bellamy, respectively) and daughter Rani (with current partner Danny Fujikawa) explained, "I actually think there are other industries where it's [more common]. Maybe modeling? I see it in business way more than I see it in Hollywood. Sometimes I've been in business meetings where I’m like, 'Wait, whose child is this? Like, this person knows nothing!'"

Ultimately, she added, "If you work hard and you kill it, it doesn't matter."

"I won't deny the privilege that I have," the model daughter of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber told Elle for a January 2023 article. "Even if it's just the fact that I have a really great source of information and someone to give me great advice, that alone I feel very fortunate for."

But when it came to making movies, the Bottoms actress said, "No artist is going to sacrifice their vision for someone's kid. That just isn't how art is made, and what I'm interested in is art."

Moreover, she added, "No one wants to work with someone who's annoying, and not easy to work with, and not kind. Yes, nepotism is prevalent, but I think if it actually was what people make it out to be, we'd see even more of it."

Carving out her own cinematic universe, Elizabeth is proof that, sometimes, it just takes one.

"I guess I understood what nepotism was like inherently as a 10-year-old," Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen's little sister, who once considered using Elizabeth Chase as her professional name, told Glamour UK in 2021. "I don’t know if I knew the word, but there is some sort of association of not earning something that I think bothered me at a very young age. It had to do with my own insecurities, but I was 10."

The son of showbiz fixtures Anne Meara and Jerry Stiller believes that a foot in the door will only get you so far.

Responding to a nepotism dig at Hopper (Sean's son) Penn, who had been cast in a short film being directed by Destry (Steven's daughter) Spielberg and written by Owen (Stephen's son) King, Stiller tweeted in 2021, "Just speaking from experience, and I don't know any of them, I would bet they all have faced challenges. Different than those with no access to the industry. Show biz as we all know is pretty rough, and ultimately is a meritocracy."

Agreeing during the exchange that Hollywood wasn't a fair playing field for a number of reasons, the Meet the Parents star clarified, "I'm saying that untalented people don't really last if they get a break because of who they are or know or are related to."

Though he got his two cents in early, the trending topic still came for Ben in February 2023 when Steve Martin called him a "nepo baby" in a teaser for their respective Pepsi Super Bowl commercials.

The former co-host of The Talk will be sure to stand by his and wife Rebecca Romijn's twin daughters Charlie and Dolly, even prepping them ahead of future criticism they may face.

“They’re going to call you a nepo baby," he recounted to Us Weekly the advice he gave. "It’s coming. The nepo baby is coming.”

He added, “You have to work for this. There’s no shortcuts. It’s going to be even harder for you!”

But he is, of course, willing to help out his daughters.

“I can sit down with my daughter who’s auditioning for a high school play at a diner, and I can say, ‘This is how you should say this line. This is how you should say this line. This is how you should say this line,’” he shared. “And it’s the only thing that I can impart on my children.”

“I can see being really pissed that I got this role, as someone else," Dylan told W after dad Sean Penn directed her in the 2021 drama Flag Day. At the same time, she added, as a working actress "I've been auditioning forever. I've been rejected forever."

Regarding the kerfuffle over her brother starring in a Spielberg-daughter-directed short, Dylan stressed, "This is the business. It is about who you know. Always. Whether you're the son of Sean Penn or not."

Hopper, who made his movie debut in Sean's film The Last Face, told E! News in February that the nepo baby conversation didn't really affect him.

"I'm like, 'If you like it, cool. If you don't, great,'" he explained, having just made Devil's Peak with mom Robin Wright. "And if you think that there's nepotism going on, I really don't care because I'm gonna do the work just as professional as everybody else, and I'm not gonna come there and do it half-ass because I'm working with my dad, I'm working with my mom.'"

Working with his father, Hopper noted, was the same "great nightmare" for him as it was for all the other actors who weren't related to the director.

And on any project, he added, "if I messed up on the film the first day, I'd be fired just like everyone else. Or, if I was terrible, I'll be terrible. And I have been terrible."

"People would always assume that if I got a job, it was because of that," the High Fidelity star told Elle in February 2022 of having Lisa Bonet and Lenny Kravitz for parents.

"That was hard," Zoë continued. "But I was incredibly privileged. I got an agent easily. I'm not going to pretend like it didn't help me get into the room. But I had to remember that I work hard, and as a child, I was putting on performances in my grandparents' house. And it had nothing to do with who my family was. It was because I loved it."

After the subject blew up, the actress told GQ months later it was "completely normal for people to be in the family business." Furthermore, she added, "It's literally where last names came from. You were a blacksmith if your family was, like, the Black family."

"People are going to have preconceived ideas about you or how you got there," the daughter of Johnny Depp and Vanessa Paradis told Elle in a November 2022 interview, "and I can definitely say that nothing is going to get you the part except for being right for the part."

Fair enough, but The Idol star's comment on the resurgent hot topic promptly launched a thousand other comments.

"I'm so careful about these conversations now," Lily-Rose told i-D a few months later. "I feel like my parents did the best job that they possibly could at giving me the most ‘normal childhood' that they could. And obviously, that still was not a normal childhood. I'm super aware of the fact that my childhood did not look like everybody's."

Responding to the discourse triggered by Lily-Rose, Kim Basinger and Alec Baldwin's daughter agreed that the kids of celebs will ultimately rise and fall on the strength of their own work. But the first rise is usually achieved thanks to a major boost.

"I wouldn't be where I am, I wouldn't have gotten where I am and been able to do what I can do if it weren't for my parents, and I think really where you go wrong is denying that," Ireland said in a November 2022 TikTok.

She got that "either you're talented, either you're capable or you're not." But "things could be a lot more simple and understandable and relatable if you just are honest about what you have and why you have what you have."

"As the child of someone, you get access other people don't have, so the playing field is not level in that way," the daughter of Blythe Danner and the late Bruce Paltrow said in July 2022 on Hailey Bieber's YouTube series Who's in My Bathroom?. "However, I really do feel that once your foot is in the door, which you unfairly got in, then you almost have to work twice as hard and be twice as good."

Bruce opened the door, directing Gwyneth in the 1989 TV movie High, her acting debut, and Steven Spielberg sprinkled pixie dust on it, casting his 14-year-old goddaughter in the 1991 Peter Pan fantasy Hook.

And that was before the debate was raging. "Now there’s this whole 'nepo baby' culture and judgment that exists around kids of famous people," Gwyneth told Bustle in October 2023, calling the term "kind of an ugly moniker."

The Dune actor—who is dad to actors Alexander Skarsgård and Bill Skarsgård—addressed the concept of nepo babies while sharing his youngest son Kolbjörn was facing criticism in school for having a famous dad.

“When his pals at school call him nepo baby, he gets so sad," he told Vulture. "He doesn’t have any friends at school. He gets isolated. Cruel kids—or cruel and ignorant. They love it on the internet.”

"But it is such a bulls--t thing," Stellan continued, "because nobody would hire you, at least not for anything good, if you’re not good enough."

Growing up with a national treasure-level star for a father, the actress and activist was acutely aware that her childhood was not normal.

"When I was 10, we moved to the East Coast, and suddenly I realized, because of how I was treated, that there was something special about me," Jane told Harvard Business Review in 2018. "It made me a little self-conscious. Some people wanted to be my friend because my father was Henry Fonda; some people didn’t like me because my father was Henry Fonda. There was both good and bad."

"When I became an actress," the two-time Oscar winner continued, "the fact that my father was a movie star was an advantage—no question—because people paid more attention to me than they would have if I were just another actress. Also, internally, I wanted to be sure that I wasn’t getting parts because I was Henry Fonda’s daughter, so I worked harder. Instead of taking one class a week, I would take four, so no one could say I was a dilettante."

"It is an amazing privilege to be a child of someone who works in an industry that you are interested in and eventually work in," the Jurassic World star—whose first role was "Redheaded Audience Girl" in dad Ron Howard's Parenthood—told The Daily Beast in 2020. "It's a privilege for that person to have success in their own right. But there was no greater privilege than the fact that my dad was supportive of me, empowered me, and showed me respect—real respect—from day one."

Naturally, Bryce continued, "insecurities can creep up or you'll hear somebody say, like, 'Oh, she only got that because of X, Y, or Z.' But that's very small."

"Put simply, I’m a nepo dad!" Ethan, who shares Maya with ex-wife Uma Thurman, cracked to Variety in September about jumping at the chance to direct his daughter in Wildcat. "And I'm not embarrassed about it."

Maya, who plays writer Flannery O'Connor in the film, said, "I had moments of insecurity about it while we were shooting the movie. But the internet doesn’t have a lot of nuances. My dad has been a massive teacher for me, and we want to work together. We like being with each other."

The 25-year-old had previously noted that she could only go so far as her parents' kid. "I think I'll get a couple chances on their name and then if I suck, I'll get kicked out of the kingdom," Maya told People in 2021. "And that's what should happen. So I'm just going to try not to suck."

Not long before she won her first Oscar for her supporting turn in Everything Everywhere All At Once, the daughter of late screen legends Tony Curtis and Janet Leigh was happy to crack a joke at the zeitgeist's expense.

"My parents were actors and I married an actor," Jamie Lee, whose husband is Christopher Guest, said while accepting her SAG Award in February 2023. "I know you'll look at me and think, 'Well, nepo baby. That's why she's there'— and I totally get it. But the truth of the matter is, I'm 64 years old and this is just amazing."

"When I was starting off, I was sort of lovingly naïve, thinking that it wasn't as big a deal as it is, that I would get the benefit of the doubt that I was my own person," Colin said of being Tom Hanks' kid on Armchair Expert in 2018. "And that doesn't happen."

The 46-year-old, whose first movie role was "Male Page" in his dad's 1996 directorial debut That Thing You Do!, said on Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend in October 2022 that he does "credit the old man" for advising him to only go into acting if he really wanted to.

Tom advised him, "'If you don't really want this, then come up with something else, 'cause you will be miserable.'"

Asked about the renewed focus on actors' actor kids, Tom—dad to Colin and daughter Elizabeth with late ex-wife Samantha Lewes and sons Chet and Truman with current spouse Rita Wilson—described showbiz as simply "the family business."

"This is what we've been doing forever," Tom told Reuters in January 2023. "It's what all of our kids grew up in. We have four kids, they're all very creative, they're all involved in some brand of storytelling."

He also acknowledged it wasn't a stretch for director Marc Forster to cast Truman as Tom's younger self in A Man Called Otto. "But the final analysis," the Oscar winner told ET at the film's premiere, "is the person has to show up on the day and hit the marks and tell the truth. Only he can make that decision. It was totally up to him."

A scion of one of the most storied Hollywood dynasties, Drew couldn't escape her famous last name.

But while being screen legend John Barrymore's granddaughter carried some weight, the Never Been Kissed star put it this way on her talk show in January 2023: "If you came from a family of lawyers, and someone said, 'Oh, well, her dad runs the firm,' it's like, 'Well, she still took the bar and got here of her own volition.' So as long as we’re not catty about it and celebratory of it, that’s the tone I want."

Heidi Klum's eldest child is perfectly fine that she's in thanks to her supermodel mom and dad Seal. But it's up to her to stay in.

"It's just a fact," Leni, 19, told People in October 2022. "My parents are famous. I did get help starting off, and I know that people would dream to start off with what I had...But I am doing the work and putting in the time. Now I'm working on my own, traveling alone, going to school. My mom and I just have the same love for the same thing."

Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann's firstborn daughter was admittedly saddened by the nepo baby tag, but she was trying not to let it get to her.

"A lot of people [in similar situations] have proven themselves over the years, so I've got to keep going and make good work," the Euphoria star told Net-a-Porter for a September 2022 article. "It's so early in my career, I don't have much to show yet, but hopefully one day I'll be really proud of the stuff I've done by myself."

"The nepo babies y'all should be worrying about are the ones working for legal firms, the ones working for banks, and the ones working in politics, If we’re talking about real world consequences and robbing people of opportunity," Allen, standing up for how hard she'd worked to get where she was, tweeted in December 2022. "BUT that’s none of my business."

In response to the inevitable backlash reminding the singer—whose parents are actor Keith Allen and film producer Alison Owen—that TikTok was focusing on entertainment nepo babies, thankyouverymuch, Lily acknowledged that was a valid conversation, too.

"It is quite clear that there is a severe lack of representation in the industry where class and race are concerned," she wrote on X, then known as Twitter. "Everyone loses as a result...I do feel that nepo babies are being somewhat scapegoated here though, there is a wider, societal conversation to be had about wealth inequality, about lack of programs and funding."

The daughter of late Sen. John McCain and Cindy McCain is of the view that there's no shame in having accomplished parents. But you gotta own it.

"To my fellow 'Nepo babies'—just acknowledge your privilege, the opportunities your last name has gotten you and move on," she offered on Instagram Stories in December 2022. "At some point talent and grit comes into play but let's stop acting like this is in anyway a rational burden that people know who [our] parents are—you sound like a--holes."

Need Stephen Baldwin's daughter (and niece of Alec, Billy and Daniel) say more than her January 2023 "Nepo Baby" tee?

"It was more so to be like, 'This is what everyone is saying and I want you to know that this is my way of responding to it,'" Hailey said in June, explaining her purposely "overly literal" message on The Circuit With Emily Chang. Indisputably a nepo baby, the Rhode Skin founder said, "I embrace that I am."

Bruce Willis and Demi Moore's youngest daughter gave big sisters Rumer Willis and Scout Willis a sartorial shout-out about being the children of movie stars in February 2023.

"Jack is really talented," the rom-com queen told Glamour of son Jack Quaid, whom she shares with ex-husband Dennis Quaid. "He's more of a natural than I'll ever be."

Meg added, "That nepo stuff is so dismissive of his work ethic, his gifts, and how sensitive he is to the idea of his privilege."

Jack is certainly aware of the assumptions that are made about the children of actors.

"I knew that people would constantly say, 'Oh, I know how he got that job,'" The Boys star told Thrillist in 2022. "And they're still going to say that. It's fine. But as long as I knew how I got there, that would be enough."

Now 31, Jack decided long ago there was no point trying to hide his parentage.

"It's not that I want to escape from it," he said on Allegedly with Matthew Cole Weiss in 2016. "I'm a huge fan of both of their work." Noting that he wasn't allowed to start auditioning until he was 18, Jack added, "If I had just parents that weren't actors, I would still be over the moon to have this job."
