Starshield has been in the news a fair bit recently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX is building and operating two satellite networks at the moment, Starlink and Starshield. What’s the difference between the two, and who uses them?

For more than a week in October 2026, Ukrainian drone operators found their high-speed satellite links shut off. Officials in Kyiv said that terminals for SpaceX’s Starshield network stopped working at speeds of above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) from Oct. 14, hampering efforts to conduct defensive operations and intercept Russian drones. Full connectivity was restored on Oct. 24, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The arguments over who did what continue, but the affair highlighted how little is publicly understood about Starshield — what it is, how it relates to Starlink, and how it is operated.

Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial, mass-market satellite internet service. The company says it now has more than 11,000 Starlink broadband and mobile satellites in orbit, operating approximately 342 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. This follows years of deployment using the company's Falcon 9 rocket..

The network serves consumers, enterprises and government customers across more than 160 countries. It is owned and operated by SpaceX. Anyone from a rural household to an airline can buy a terminal and a service plan.

Governments are also customers, with public agencies using Starlink for a range of purposes including connectivity, disaster response and national security, notably in the case of Ukraine in the wake of the invasion by Russia, which began in February 2022 and is ongoing.

Starshield is SpaceX’s network for serving national security customers. The company announced the program in December 2022, stating it would apply Starlink technology and SpaceX's launch capability to government needs, initially in three areas: Earth observation, communications and hosted payloads.

"They are using the same satellite buses," says Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. “They look the same, but they have a lot more kit on them that allows them to do more things. They provide similar broadband internet, but with more secure hardware and software and hardened systems.”

The company says it has won multi-billion-dollar, multiyear contracts from the U.S. military in 2026 for Starshield-related services.

Some Starshield satellites may also carry sensors for intelligence and surveillance. But much about Starshield is secretive, with its finances not revealed and launches often classified.

Starshield is made up of a range of different assets, including spy satellites, military data satellites, and secure communications for ground users.

The spy satellites are sent into orbit in launches for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), for a "proliferated architecture" of spy satellites, including electro-optical, radar and relay spacecraft. The NRO does not use the Starshield name, but said earlier this year that it had launched more than 200 satellites in recent years, many of which are for its proliferated architecture.

Then there is the Space Data Network Backbone. The U.S. Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion fixed-price contract to build the network, previously known as MILNET, using Starshield satellites. It is meant to move data quickly between missile-warning sensors and interceptors as part of the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense plan. A prototype is due by the end of 2027. A Space Force official has described MILNET as government-owned and operated by SpaceX as a contractor, under Space Force oversight.

Starshield provides encrypted connectivity for military users through terminals. These can be dedicated Starshield terminals, or Starlink terminals for Starshield services.

Crucially, the networks overlap. "Those Starshield satellites are physically separate from Starlink satellites, but the Starshield satellites can use the Starlink network if they need to," Bowen said. That interoperability is available to U.S. national security users, he added, "but not if you're a commercial user of Starlink."

Use restrictions differ, too. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said that Starlink's terms of service bar its use for offensive drone strikes, while decisions about Starshield use rest with the U.S. government.

Who controls Starshield is a question that entered the public consciousness in the wake of the Ukraine Starshield speed limit affair. The U.S. government is the customer, and also in some cases the owner, but SpaceX builds the satellites, operates the underlying Starlink network on which some Starshield services run and, in some arrangements, operates the Starshield satellites themselves. How this command is divided between the government and SpaceX is unclear.

Bowen compared it to the U.K.’s Skynet military satellite system, in which contractor Babcock operates the satellites. "The actual button punching is done by the contractors, but the military and government are in the room and are calling the shots,” he said.

That question matters, because it determines whether SpaceX can act on its own or only with government oversight and approval.

Starshield appears set to become more central to U.S. military space. The Space Data Network Backbone prototype is expected next year, while NRO launches will continue, according to contracts. With SpaceX now a public company, quarterly reports could provide more insight into the system. For now, however, much remains classified.

#645. Khloe Kardashian Details Finding Lamar Odom in 20-Person "Circle Jerk”

Khloe Kardashian and Kris Jenner recalled finding Lamar Odom in a 20-person “circle jerk” during the Nov. 5 episode of The Kardashians: “The most crazy thing that Khloe and I ever did.”

Khloe Kardashian fought for her marriage with Lamar Odom—quite literally.

Kris Jenner took a stroll down memory lane during the Nov. 5 episode of The Kardashians, recalling an evening when she and her daughter barged in on the NBA player in a hotel room amid his challenges with substance abuse.

“The most crazy thing that Khloe and I ever did was she realized that her significant other at the time, Lamar, was smoking crack,” Jenner—who had taken an edible ahead of filming the scene—told the group consisting of Kim Kardashian, Nikki Glaser, Brenda Song and Fortune Feimster. “We had intel that he was going to be at a certain hotel. Khloe goes, ‘Okay, we're gonna get him.’ And I'm like, ‘Okay.’ She goes, ‘Dress in black, hoodie, with a beanie.’”

Meanwhile, the Good American founder took some issue with her mom’s recollection of events. After sarcastically remarking during a confessional, “This is a good story I want to bring up right now,” she told the gathered group it was really Jenner who “put the drama on” with the all-black outfits.

“I just said, ‘We’re going to get Lamar,’” Kardashian emphasized. “That’s all I said.”

But the matriarch’s storytelling was not to be deterred, regaling the captivated audience with her dramatically rendered recollection of events.

“We’re gonna extract him from the situation because he’s being held hostage by these hookers,” Jenner said. “We were in the hotel going down the hallways, and Khloe’s security burst into this room.”

Which is when Kardashian supplied the following detail: “They were literally having a circle jerk.”

Yes, as Kardashian—who was married to Odom for seven years before their 2016 split—claimed, there were approximately 20 people in this hotel room participating in group sex.

The sight, according to Jenner, immediately took the wind out of her spy-like sails.

“I went from Charlie’s Angles to, ‘Ah!’” she exclaimed, adding of Kardashian, “She runs into the room like she's Hawaii Five-O. She's like, ‘Okay, everyone, like, basically hands up.’”

This piece of her story was corroborated by Kardashian, who said she did indeed “start swinging” at the individuals inside the room.

“My mom is hiding in the bathroom,” she said. “She's getting a trash can, and she's like, ‘Okay, honey, keep going.’ And she's literally swiping all of the drugs, everything in trash bags.”

As for who Kardashian was punching? As she told the inquiring Feimster, “Random whores, I never even introduced myself.”

The unexpected retelling of this particular moment in her life made Kardashian—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Tristan Thompson—do some reflecting on what she’s really looking for in a future man.

“This is solidifying how I will never date a freak again,” she said in a confessional. “I didn't even know I needed to put this on my manifest list, but maybe I should add no circle jerks, no orgies, and like maybe no hardcore drugs.”

While Odom is firmly in her past, read on for an update on the love life of Kardashian and the rest of the Kardashian-Jenner family.

Why, yes, Kris Jenner and longtime love Corey Gamble are still doing amazing, sweetie. In 2014, the music industry insider approached the world's most famous momager at fashion designer Riccardo Tisci's 40th birthday bash in Ibiza and "I just tried saying, 'You're beautiful. I'd love to get to know you,'" he shared on the family's OG series, Keeping Up With the Kardashians, "and it went from there."

More than a decade in, Kris gushed about her "ride or die" in a 2025 birthday tribute, writing, "Thank you for all you do every single day, for the love you give, and for always being there for all of us. I’m so blessed to have you by my side."

With all due respect for all the small things, Kourtney Kardashian's husband has made some pretty grand gestures throughout their yearlong marriage. Take her 44th birthday that saw her and Travis Barker take a trip up the California coast to Santa Barbara. The Blink-182 drummer marked the occasion by filling their room at the famed Kennedy Cottage with rose petals and gifting her with a $161,819 piece by artist Yoshitomo Nara. The Poosh founder has fully embraced her new life as the girl at the rock show. And in November 2023, she and Travis welcomed their first child together, son Rocky Thirteen Barker.

As Kim Kardashian put it in The Kardashians trailer, "Things change really quickly." When season two wrapped, the SKIMS founder was still with then-Saturday Night Live standout Pete Davidson.

She got fans hoping she was getting back in the dating game with retired NFL quarterback Tom Brady.

Alas, the mom to North West, Saint West, Chicago West and Psalm West—with ex-husband Kanye West—wasn't on the hunt for a new teammate, a source telling E! News in May 2023, "They have friends and business partners in common."

By early 2026, she was racing into a new romance with Lewis Hamilton, hard-launching her relationship with the F1 driver that June.

After her divorce, she told The Times in October, "I wanted to completely heal and just work on myself. I wasn't ready to open up. I really wasn't even thinking about it. The universe works in your favor when you just allow it to."

In a 2023 episode, Kris shoots her shot while chatting with Khloe Kardashian about Tristan Thompson, asking, "How's everything going with Tristan?" Safe to say the Good American founder has the basketball player benched for now. Though the exes have worked out a game plan for raising daughter True and son Tatum, Khloe shot down the idea that they're back together in May 2023, calling the narrative "tiring."

She's more interested in starting a fresh story. After meeting Love Is Blind star Alexa Lemieux the following April, Khloe pitched a winning idea to Netflix, writing on Instagram, "I think some of us single K sisters should go on LIB. What do you think?"

Months after Kendall Jenner's split with NBA guard Devin Booker in fall 2022, the model's love life got an assist from friends Justin Bieber and Hailey Bieber. The married duo were spotted enjoying a double date with the reality star and musician Bad Bunny in February 2023. The following December, it was reported that the two had called it quits.

Then in the spring of 2026, fans started to wonder if a new romance was in bloom as Kendall was spotted hanging out with Jacob Elordi. The Euphoria alum was among those cheering for the model when she walked in Milan Fashion Week in September 2026.

Seems Kylie Jenner has found herself a new beautiful boy. Last seen publicly with rapper Travis Scott—dad to her daughter Stormi and son Aire—at an Art Basel party in December 2022, the beauty mogul, has first linked to Oscar-nominated actor Timothée Chalamet in April 2023.

Now, rise and shine because you don't want to miss the glimpses they've given us of their romance at New York Fashion Week and the US Open, as well as live on TV, when they showed PDA while seated together at the 2024 Golden Globes and 2025 Oscars.

Then, while accepting Best Actor at the 2026 Critics Choice Awards in January, he thanked his "partner of three years," for the foundation she provides, adding, "I couldn't do this without you. Thank you from the bottom of my heart."

#644. Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive

At first glance it looks exactly like a seahorse. It has the same horse-shaped head tilted down from the body, the same curled and grasping tail, and in the males a fully enclosed pouch for brooding the young.

But this little fish, no longer than your thumb, is not a seahorse, as we report in our new study published in the Journal of Lost Species. This is Australyichthys aegis, a newly described fish from the deep reefs off southern Australia. We have given it the common name helmethead sea muppet, after the domed, helmet-like crest on its head.

Its scientific name follows the same idea: in Greek mythology the aegis was a protective shield. Together with its two relatives, the bullneck sea muppet (A. minotaur) and the paradoxical sea muppet (A. paradoxus), it makes up a small group we nickname the sea muppets.

All three, we have now shown, belong on their own branch of the family tree. The seahorse look has arisen more than once, and these fish are a case of it evolving well away from the true seahorses. That evidence had been sitting in museum drawers, misfiled, for decades.

You will not find these fish while scuba diving.

Every known specimen was brought up by accident, caught in trawl nets or dredges working the seafloor between about 50 and 125 meters down. The single specimen of A. aegis came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf.

The dredge that caught it was sampling for small shelled animals known as brachiopods during a natural history expedition. Because that expedition was after invertebrates, the fish was mistakenly catalogued into the invertebrate collection of the South Australian Museum, where it sat unrecognized for years.

After each chance capture the fish were preserved, then largely forgotten. The rest are held in Australian museum collections, among them the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO.

The whole genus is known from just seven specimens gathered over about 65 years, scattered across more than 2,500 kilometers of coastline, and nothing has been collected in nearly two decades.

The specimens are irreplaceable, so we could not dissect them. Instead we used micro-CT scanning, the same X-ray technology used in hospitals but fine enough to resolve tiny bones.

That let us build three-dimensional models of each fish’s skeleton and compare them bone by bone with true seahorses (Hippocampus).

Every earlier assessment had rested on external appearance, and the skeletons did not support it. Seahorses have a particular internal architecture, including a rigid cage of fused bony plates supporting the belly and a bony crown, called a coronet, on the head.

Our scans showed that Australyichthys has neither. In their place is a different arrangement of bones supporting the belly, one that appears in no seahorse.

A. aegis had been fixed in ethanol rather than formalin, the only member of the genus stored that way, and ethanol leaves genetic material intact. Sequencing it placed the fish well outside the seahorses, on the branch that is their closest relative. The genes said what the bones had already said.

All three species had been placed in the seahorse genus on the strength of how they look, and on that evidence they were seahorses. They are not, and they needed a genus of their own. We named it Australyichthys, from the Latin for southern and the Greek for fish.

When separate lineages evolve to look alike, biologists call it convergent evolution, and it usually reflects a shared way of life rather than shared ancestry.

The whole seahorse body, with its bent head, gripping tail and brood pouch, has been built at least twice within a single fish family, the Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons.

Working out how that happened may reveal why evolution keeps arriving at the same solution.

All this happened along the Great Southern Reef, the connected system of kelp forests and rocky reefs that rings southern Australia. Many of its species are found nowhere else, and its deeper zones are barely explored.

In fact, an entire genus of vertebrate hid there, misidentified, until a CT scanner settled the question.

No one has ever seen one of these fish alive; they have turned up only by chance in a passing net or dredge. On that record they now qualify as lost species, known from a handful of preserved animals and never from a living one.

Calling them lost is not a prediction of extinction. It marks them as a priority for targeted surveys that go looking rather than waiting for the next accidental catch. They are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Graham Short and David Harasti. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#642. Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken

Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in almost the opposite way of previously known defenses. The surprising mechanism allows bacteria to activate a deadly self-destruct process when viruses attack, potentially offering new ideas for developing medical treatments and gene-editing technologies.

The findings, published in Molecular Cell, reveal how a group of bacterial defense systems called "type VI retrons" use an unexpectedly complex sequence of molecular events to fight infection. Unlike other retrons, these systems rely on DNA to activate a toxin rather than keep one suppressed.

Understanding this unusual process could do more than expand scientists' knowledge of bacterial immunity. It may also provide a foundation for designing more effective DNA-editing tools, potentially allowing researchers to correct harmful genetic mutations with greater precision.

"This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across," says Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, senior author of the new study. "These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we'll use in future technologies."

How Bacteria Sacrifice Themselves to Stop Viruses

Bacteria face constant threats from viruses known as phages, which infect bacterial cells and use their machinery to reproduce. Over time, bacteria have evolved a variety of defenses to prevent these viruses from spreading.

Among these defenses are retrons, molecular systems that can detect certain viral infections and trigger the infected bacterium to destroy itself. Although this sacrifice kills the individual cell, it prevents the virus from producing more copies and infecting nearby bacteria, helping protect the larger colony.

Retrons are also of considerable interest to scientists developing new genetic technologies. They can efficiently produce and deliver single-stranded DNA, making them promising tools for editing DNA inside human cells. Shipman's team and other researchers are investigating whether these capabilities could eventually be used to correct mutations responsible for disease with exceptional accuracy.

Until now, scientists believed they understood the basic way retron defenses operate.

In previously studied retrons, a toxic protein is already present inside an uninfected cell, but its harmful effects are held in check by short pieces of single-stranded DNA. When a phage infects the bacterium, it disrupts this protective arrangement, allowing the toxin to act. The resulting cell death prevents the virus from spreading.

The newly investigated type VI retrons, however, did not appear to follow this familiar pattern.

A Bacterial Immune System That Works Backward

Researchers first became suspicious that type VI retrons were different when they could not detect the single-stranded DNA normally associated with these systems.

"The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA," says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman's lab and lead author of the study. "But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn't appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken."

Despite their unusual behavior, experiments showed that bacteria carrying type VI retrons could still defend themselves against phage infections. The systems were clearly functional, even though they lacked the expected molecular signs of activity.

"That kicked off a long molecular odyssey," Shipman says. "Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work."

After extensive investigation, the team discovered that type VI retrons reverse a key step in the usual defense process.

Rather than maintaining a substantial supply of single-stranded DNA and toxin before infection, these retrons produce little detectable DNA and no noticeable amount of toxin in healthy cells. The arrival of a phage triggers a sharp increase in DNA production.

As the DNA accumulates, it interacts with an RNA molecule that has been preventing the toxin from being made. This interaction removes the restriction, allowing the bacterium to rapidly produce the toxic protein.

The toxin appears to be an exceptionally small protein that inserts itself into the bacterium's surrounding cell membrane. By disrupting the membrane's stability, it causes the infected cell to die, stopping the viral infection from spreading.

In other words, the DNA acts as an activation switch rather than a restraint. Instead of preventing an existing toxin from causing harm, it helps turn on toxin production only when the bacterium detects a threat.

"It's almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin," Zhang says. "It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system -- whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they're a stepping stone between different types."

An Unusual Discovery Required New Experiments

Figuring out how type VI retrons function proved unusually difficult. Many established techniques that scientists use to examine retrons repeatedly produced no useful results, forcing the team to develop new experimental strategies and adapt existing methods.

One particularly important challenge involved detecting the DNA produced by type VI retrons in cells that had not been infected.

After conventional tests failed, the researchers tried a technique called Spacer-seq, which had previously been developed in Shipman's laboratory. The method uses components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to record molecular activity inside cells.

CRISPR-Cas is best known for its role in modern gene-editing technologies, but bacteria originally evolved these systems as defenses against viruses. Spacer-seq takes advantage of this natural machinery to help researchers investigate what happens inside cells.

The alternative approach finally revealed a trace amount of single-stranded DNA that earlier experiments had missed.

"We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells," Zhang says.

This breakthrough encouraged the researchers to continue investigating. Additional experiments confirmed that type VI retrons produce DNA at very low levels under normal conditions and substantially increase production only after a phage enters the cell.

The findings explained why the defense system had appeared inactive in earlier tests and revealed the unusual sequence of events responsible for its antiviral activity.

Could This Strange Bacterial Defense Lead to New Medical Treatments?

The discovery is already influencing research in Shipman's laboratory, where scientists are exploring ways to transform the type VI retron's natural machinery into useful technologies.

One promising application involves developing synthetic molecular sensors and switches that can regulate gene activity. Such systems could potentially allow researchers to control when particular genes are activated or suppressed, opening new possibilities for studying disease and designing treatments.

"This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before," Zhang says. "Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate."

Another possibility involves the retron's unusually small but powerful toxins. Because these proteins can disrupt bacterial membranes and kill cells, researchers are investigating whether they could be adapted into new antimicrobial treatments.

Such therapies could potentially target harmful bacteria responsible for human infections, providing a new approach to combating bacterial disease.

These medical applications remain under development, but the discovery offers researchers a molecular design that would have been difficult to imagine without studying nature's existing solutions.

"This study highlights why it's so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration," Shipman says. "We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize."

The research also raises intriguing questions about bacterial evolution, including how such an elaborate defense arose and whether type VI retrons represent an earlier, later, or intermediate stage in the evolution of these immune systems.

For scientists seeking new ways to manipulate DNA, control genes, and fight infections, this backward-acting bacterial defense could provide an unexpected starting point.

The research, "Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein," was published in Molecular Cell on October 13, 2026.

Along with Shipman and Zhang, the authors include Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, and Alejandro González-Delgado of Gladstone; Josepha Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis Zhang, Mario Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Guillermo Montoya, and Rafael Pinilla-Redondo of the University of Copenhagen; and Lieza Chan and Kliment Verba of UC San Francisco.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. Kleberg Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Fulbright U.S. Student Program, the Junta de Castilla y León and European Social Fund Plus, the European Molecular Biology Organization, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the European Research Council, and the Villum Foundation.

#641. 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart

A small, circular hole in a 75,000-year-old Neanderthal shoulder blade may reveal one of the earliest known cases of deadly violence involving a wooden spear. The remarkable discovery, made in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, suggests that the individual was struck by a sharpened wooden weapon that passed through the chest, potentially in a deliberate attack aimed at the heart.

Researchers believe the wound could represent the oldest evidence in the hominin fossil record of fatal interpersonal violence involving a wooden spear.

The shoulder blade (scapula) is an unusually delicate bone, with some areas so thin that light can pass through them. Despite its fragile structure, the Neanderthal's bone survived for approximately 75,000 years beneath seven and a half meters of rock and sediment. Almost the entire bone remained intact, except for a remarkably precise circular opening measuring 15 millimeters across.

A Deadly Spear Wound Reveals a Neanderthal's Violent Death

Archaeologists from the University of Cambridge, who led the excavation, believe the hole was created by a spear with a sharpened wooden point. Its rounded shape is an important clue because weapons tipped with flint or stone generally produce openings with flatter or more angular edges.

Their reconstruction suggests that the spear entered the front of the Neanderthal's left chest, passed through a lung and probably major blood vessels, and continued until it pierced the shoulder blade from behind. Such a severe injury would have caused rapid death. The researchers suspect the blow may have been an intentional "heart shot."

The physical evidence offers additional clues about how the attack occurred. The opening has beveled edges, a feature commonly associated with an exit wound. Small bone fragments displaced during the impact indicate that the weapon likely entered from above and traveled downward through the body.

Using these fragments, the scientists were able to partially reconstruct the damaged area. Subtle ridges left by muscle attachments helped them determine where the pieces originally belonged.

"It's extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don't get complete scapulae from modern burials," said Dr. Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology. "We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight meters of rock and sediment."

The remains have been named Shanidar A after the cave where they were uncovered. The findings were published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Ancient Wooden Spears Were Sophisticated Hunting Weapons

Although sharpened wooden weapons were used hundreds of thousands of years ago, relatively few examples have survived. Wood usually decays over time, making it exceptionally difficult for archaeologists to recover evidence of ancient woodworking and weapon technology.

One important discovery occurred in the 1990s at Schöningen, Germany, where researchers uncovered wooden spears preserved in waterlogged conditions. Dating back roughly 200,000 years, these weapons were made during a period when early Neanderthals inhabited Europe.

Some measured more than two meters in length. Their makers carefully selected the wood and shaped the spears to achieve a balance suitable for throwing, much like modern javelins. Archaeologists believe they were probably used to hunt large animals.

Even older evidence comes from Clacton-on-Sea in the United Kingdom. In 1911, a pointed wooden fragment was recovered from the shoreline and later identified as part of a spear more than 400,000 years old. Only its tip had survived, making it the earliest known example of a rounded wooden spear.

The Cambridge researchers believe comparable weapons could have been responsible for Shanidar A's death. If their interpretation is correct, the injury may provide the first evidence that sharpened wooden spears were used in the prehistoric Middle East.

"Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula," said Pomeroy, a fellow at Newnham College, Cambridge. "That early technology absolutely works for this wound."

"What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A. This package of capabilities could have spanned the full range of Neanderthal homelands, from Wales to Siberia."

The discovery raises a difficult question: Was Shanidar A the victim of a deliberate attack, or did a hunting accident cause the fatal injury?

Pomeroy acknowledges that accidents involving wooden spears would have been possible, particularly when Neanderthals hunted large, dangerous animals at close range.

"Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it's easy to imagine lethal injuries."

Nevertheless, certain features of the wound suggest that the blow may have been intentional rather than accidental.

"The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal's body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart."

The researchers cannot determine exactly what happened or who wielded the weapon. It is also impossible to establish whether modern humans played any role. However, they consider violence between Neanderthals the simplest explanation consistent with the available evidence.

"All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal's life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear," said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, who leads the Shanidar Cave excavations.

"Evidence of systematic violence is extremely rare in deep prehistory. The vast majority comes from periods of settled farming communities thousands of years after hunter-gather societies like our Neanderthals."

A Shattered Tooth Reveals a Surprising Story of Compassion

Although Shanidar A appears to have died violently, other evidence suggests this individual received considerable care earlier in life.

Alongside the shoulder blade, archaeologists recovered a nearly complete right hand, two ribs from the left side, a fragment of a right rib, and seven teeth. Together, these are the surviving remains of an adult Neanderthal believed to have been approximately 45 years old at death.

One tooth provides particularly revealing evidence about the individual's life. An incisor from the front of the lower jaw had been split vertically, leaving just half of the tooth intact. Neighboring teeth had also been forced inward.

Researchers believe the damage resulted from a powerful blow to the face. The surviving half of the incisor had accumulated substantial tartar (dental calculus) along its exposed root canal, indicating that the damaged tooth remained in the mouth for an extended period after the injury.

This buildup suggests that Shanidar A survived the original trauma rather than dying immediately. Such extensive facial damage would likely have made eating and communicating extremely painful and difficult.

"Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals," said Pomeroy.

The researchers suggest that other members of the group may have helped Shanidar A survive by providing softer foods. Earlier studies of sediments from Shanidar Cave found evidence that Neanderthals were soaking plant foods before cooking them around this period.

This method of food preparation could have made meals easier for someone suffering from severe facial injuries.

"There's no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time."

For the scientists, these findings reveal two seemingly opposite aspects of Neanderthal behavior in the life of a single individual.

"The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognize as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime."

Prof Barker said: "It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual."

Shanidar Cave Is Transforming Our Understanding of Neanderthals

Shanidar Cave, situated in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, has played a major role in changing scientific views of Neanderthal behavior.

During the 1950s, excavations led by archaeologist Ralph Solecki uncovered the remains of ten Neanderthals. Four individuals were found grouped together in the same location, even though they had died at different times.

Their placement suggested that Neanderthals may have repeatedly returned to a particular part of the cave to bury their dead.

Another remarkable discovery from a different section of the cave involved a Neanderthal who lived thousands of years later. This individual had experienced serious physical disabilities, including a paralyzed arm, arthritis, hearing loss, and partial blindness.

Despite these conditions, the individual survived to an advanced age, suggesting that other members of the community provided assistance and care.

Discoveries like these helped overturn the image of Neanderthals that prevailed during the Victorian era, when they were often portrayed as primitive, brutish, and less than fully human.

Subsequent research has revealed increasingly sophisticated behavior, including cave art and jewelry. Genetic studies have also established that Neanderthals interbred with modern humans, leaving traces of their DNA in populations alive today.

Evidence Suggests Neanderthals Returned to Bury Their Dead

Shanidar A, excavated in 2020, adds another important piece to this growing picture of Neanderthal society.

Since 2015, the Cambridge-led archaeological team has identified three additional Neanderthals within the cave's previously known cluster of remains. These discoveries bring the number of individuals in that particular burial area to five, consisting of four adults and one infant.

All five were found within an extraordinarily confined space measuring approximately 1.5 meters long, one meter wide, and one meter deep.

The location lies immediately behind a large upright boulder that researchers describe as a "prominent marker." Thin layers of sediment separate the individual sets of remains, indicating that the bodies were deposited at different times.

Shanidar A was discovered at the greatest depth within the cluster and may have been the first individual placed there. The body was positioned on its back, with the head pointing east. The Neanderthal found directly above it had been arranged in a similar position.

These patterns suggest that the cave's occupants were not simply leaving bodies wherever space was available. Instead, they may have deliberately chosen a particular location and returned to it repeatedly to lay deceased members of their community to rest.

"The best explanation is intentional and symbolic funerary behavior," said Pomeroy. "These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest. Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades."

Taken together, the discoveries at Shanidar Cave paint a complex picture of Neanderthal life 75,000 years ago. The same individual who may have died in a deliberate spear attack had apparently survived a devastating earlier injury with the help of others and was eventually placed in a location that may have held special significance for the community.

Far from fitting the outdated stereotype of Neanderthals as simple, brutal creatures, Shanidar A provides rare physical evidence of a society capable of both deadly violence and sustained compassion.

White Vision, Hex Vision, and Ultron all converge in this spirited new superhero series.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Marvel Studios' existential superhero series "VisionQuest" has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers.

The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's "WandaVision" and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps.

And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest.

Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned!

We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is.

Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods.

*This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest.

We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger.

From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision.

One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision.

So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one.

So, the Vision we see in "VisionQuest" is the physical body of White Vision, injected with thoughts and remembrances of the model that was magically resurrected by Wanda. Confused yet? Don't worry, it's going to get weirder.

In addition to the two versions of Vision from "WandaVision," numerous other AIs exist within Vision's skull and are all represented by human avatars acting as factions of his ravaged psyche.

Cast your mind all the way back to 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and you'll remember that Vision was conceived from a combination of the artificial brain of Ultron, the Mind Stone, and fragments of Tony Stark’s AI butler companion, J.A.R.V.I.S., who was named after the real Jarvis seen in the "Agent Carter" TV series.

J.A.R.V.I.S. appears in "VisionQuest" as his own unique entity, alongside another of Tony Stark's AI helpers, E.D.I.T.H., aka the AI in the smart glasses that Stark left to Peter Parker after his death. She shows up in "Spider-Man: Far From Home," which is a great movie but not an essential viewing if you're preparing for "VisionQuest."

Then let's toss in the fact that papa Ultron (James Spader) is buzzing around in Vision’s cranium, creating what’s been described as more or less an "Age of Ultron" and a "WandaVision" sequel at the same time. As it turns out, Vision did not destroy Ultron at the end of "Age of Ultron"; he copied his code and absorbed him, so now the rabid robot lives on in Vision’s brain.

The show’s narrative is centered around the complicated relationship between Vision and his son Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Tommy was created by Wanda's Hex and should have disappeared when it collapsed, but both he and his brother Billy survived through magical shenanigans that are explained in 2024's "Agatha All Along."

Those two Maximoff boys, Tommy and Billy, both vanished from existence at the conclusion of "WandaVision." "Agatha All Along" exposed the truth that their consciousnesses entered the ether before expiring, only to reemerge into the souls of two teenage boys who had just perished, therefore returning them to life. Are you still with us? Good, just checking.

The finale of "Agatha All Along" hinted at the return of the estranged Tommy, and "VisionQuest" dives into that dangling plot point with relish!

Every show needs an antagonist, and the voices in Vision's head can't do all the work. "VisionQuest" has introduced a duo of villains for Vision to contend with. Neither of them has shown up in the MCU previously, though, so you don't need to do any research here.

With a massive bounty on his head after breaking free from S.W.O.R.D.'s control, White Vision must contend with a new villainous foe in the form of a mysterious mercenary named Paladin (Todd Stashwick).

This enigmatic Marvel Comics character was created by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino and was first seen prowling the pages of "Daredevil #150" back in 1978. He's basically a gun-for-hire in the Marvel universe, often hired to fight alongside or against various heroes depending on the story. We don't know much about his motivations in the show, but we'll learn more as it goes on.

"VisionQuest" also shines a spotlight on the bizarro character of Ultron's "bride," Jocasta, though the MCU version of this character diverges wildly from the comic book inspiration.

It's enough to drive one to madness! Between all the father-son dynamics dancing around the eight scheduled episodes, being hunted down by mercs, and his transcendent search for meaning, Vision and his saga are hopefully headed to a peaceful end.

Created by Terry Matalas ("Star Trek: Picard," "12 Monkeys") and airing two new chapters each Tuesday night on Disney+, VisionQuest is bolstered by a cast that includes Ruaridh Mollica, T'Nia Miller, Lauren Morais, Orla Brady, Diane Morgan, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy.

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1.

Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station.

During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays. They left on the space shuttle Discovery, which brought up the Expedition 2 crew that would take their place.

As of today, there has been a continuous astronaut presence in space aboard the International Space Station for 26 years. For all of these years, not a day has gone by without someone living in space, orbiting our planet from aboard the space station.

While the ISS was not the first space station, it has been the longest-running space statin by far. This first crew were pioneers, showing how humans could actually live and work aboard this station. This exploratory mission proved that the station could successfully support astronaut crews.

Since this mission 26 years ago, there have been literally hundreds of astronauts from around the world who have flown to and lived aboard the ISS. While NASA has stated that the station might be decommissioned in the coming years, these accomplishments will remain forever in spaceflight history.

#638. Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way certain metals can withstand extreme cold without becoming dangerously brittle. The discovery challenges long-standing ideas about how metals behave at extremely low temperatures and could help engineers develop tougher materials for some of the harshest environments imaginable.

The findings, published October 14 in Nature, reveal a previously unknown microscopic process that allows two experimental metal alloys to remain remarkably resistant to damage at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C (-424°F). The research was led by an international team from the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford.

Why Extreme Cold Makes Some Metals Brittle

Cooling a metal generally increases its strength, but this improvement can come with a serious drawback. Certain metals become increasingly brittle as temperatures fall, making them more likely to crack or break instead of bending under pressure.

This problem is particularly important for a family of materials known as body-centered cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten, and chromium). Their atoms are arranged in a specific crystal pattern that can make them especially vulnerable to brittle failure in extreme cold. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, a small crack that might ordinarily be accommodated by the metal changing shape can instead spread and cause a fracture.

However, researchers discovered that two experimental alloys made from niobium and titanium behave very differently. Even when cooled to -253°C, both materials maintained an impressive ability to withstand damage. Neither showed a measurable shift toward brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested.

The explanation lies in a surprising change in how the metals respond to stress. Rather than relying on their usual method of deformation, the alloys activate a different microscopic process that helps prevent cracks from spreading.

A Hidden Mechanism Helps Metals Resist Cracking

Under normal conditions, body-centered cubic metals bend and change shape through the movement of tiny defects within their crystal structures. These defects, called dislocations, allow layers of atoms to shift relative to one another, helping the material absorb stress without breaking.

As temperatures drop, however, these dislocations become increasingly difficult to move. With fewer ways to accommodate the forces concentrated around a crack, the metal becomes more likely to fracture.

The newly studied alloys have another way to respond.

Researchers observed a process called nanoscale 'twinning', in which tiny sections of the metal's crystal structure rearrange into mirror-image patterns. This occurs alongside a localized change in the crystal structure itself.

When these newly formed regions encounter the boundaries separating neighboring crystals, they produce concentrated areas of stress. Those stress concentrations generate additional defects, giving the metal new opportunities to deform rather than crack.

The researchers compare this behavior to a road system finding alternative routes when its usual roads become blocked by ice. As extreme cold makes conventional deformation increasingly difficult, the newly formed crystal structures provide other pathways for the metal to accommodate stress.

By creating these new pathways, the material can continue absorbing forces around potential fractures instead of failing abruptly.

A Breakthrough for Metals Used in Extreme Environments

The findings suggest a new approach to developing structural metals that can withstand exceptionally low temperatures. Such materials could be valuable in energy systems, transportation, and aerospace engineering, where components may encounter severe thermal conditions.

Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu (Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford) said: "For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application."

The discovery also changes how scientists may need to think about what determines whether a metal becomes brittle. Previously, much of the emphasis was placed on how easily existing defects could travel through a material. The new results indicate that generating fresh defects may be just as important.

Lead author Dr. David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures."

To investigate how the alloys performed under such punishing conditions, the team conducted experiments using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire.

The researchers used gaseous helium to cool metal samples to approximately -253°C. While directing a beam of neutrons through the materials, they used a specialized testing machine to stretch the samples by pulling from opposite ends.

This setup allowed the team to measure the forces the metals could withstand and determine how far they could stretch before breaking. The neutron measurements also helped researchers investigate what was happening inside the materials as they were deformed.

Afterward, the scientists examined the tested samples using powerful electron microscopes. These instruments revealed extremely small structural changes within the metal, including those near cracks that helped explain its unusual resistance to damage.

The team also used atom-probe analysis to determine how individual elements were distributed throughout the alloys. Combined with computer modeling, these measurements helped establish how the different microscopic processes worked together to prevent brittle failure.

The results offer more than an explanation for the surprising behavior of two experimental alloys. They identify a potentially useful strategy for designing metals that can remain tough even when conventional methods of deformation stop working, opening new possibilities for technologies that must operate in extreme cold.

The international collaboration included researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#637. ‘A Vast Landgrab’: ICMP Weighs-In on Big AI’s Australian Copyright Battleground

"We need to refuse OpenAI, Anthropic and Big Tech's asks and instead focus on enforcement," Phelan explains.

SYDNEY, Australia — As Australia’s leadership considers rewrites to the nation’s copyright laws that would allow for AI training, the land down under finds itself front and center in the creative industries’ most pressing issue.

It’s a fast-moving target. OpenAI, Anthropic and others have tirelessly lobbied the federal government for changes in the copyright act that would enable the tech companies to train AI models in these parts.   Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

Should big AI get the win, the music industry has warned, a potential doomsday scenario could unfold for the arts.

“Done the way that Big AI is proposing,” ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd remarked in October, “it would devastate the music industry and make Australia a pariah for rights holders globally.”

Earlier, in July, prime minister Anthony Albanese had given assurances that tech and AI companies couldn’t use copyright-protected works including consent, credit and compensation, broadly in with the message from the music community.

A kind of smackdown was delivered Oct. 13, however, when Jo Briskey and Jono Duniam, co-chairs of the joint parliamentary committee for AI, suggested that Australia’s existing copyright law wasn’t up the scratch and that, without fresh changes, creators would miss out in the AI age.

Not only was the statement “wrong,” Herd said at the time, but “it ignores substantial evidence provided to the Committee. Australian copyright law gives creators control. It is the only thing standing between major American AI companies and unchecked access to the world’s content right here from Australia.”

In the digital era, implores the labels association and other creative industry trade bodies, the world’s music, books, journalism, films, photographs and other copyright material published online are at risk under the proposals.

The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) agrees with the assessment.

“This is a vast landgrab,” explains John Phelan, director general of the Brussels-based ICMP, which represents 90% of the world’s commercially released music and whose members include Universal Music Publishing Group, Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell Music, BMG, Kobalt, Reservoir and Concord Music Publishing, alongside thousands of other indie publishers. “We say they must play by the same Australian and international laws as all other AI companies who respect the rules and so our industry licenses.”

Earlier in 2026, APRA AMCOS hosted the CISAC board of directors in Sydney. AI was at the top of the agenda. Billboard recently caught up with Phelan for an update on an issue whose “implications are global.”

Billboard: Just how concerned should the international music community be, and why should the situation in Australia — of all places — deserve our attention?

John Phelan: What’s on the table is a plan, cooked as much in Silicon Valley as Sydney, to enable tech and AI companies to utilize the world’s digital music for ingestion and training.

The downstream GenAI product would be paid for. But the proposal is still as commercially and legally harmful as could be. The mitigation mechanism being placed under the prime minister’s nose is an opt out system. But this cannot work. The ideas have gained a lot of traction by politicians at the highest level, due to a combination of eagerness to act on AI markets and other interests.

But make no mistake, this is subordination dressed up as sovereignty. It must not meet legal ink.

ICMP has data on how these AI companies have scraped enormous volumes of content. It would appear they’re using the tactic “best to ask for forgiveness than to ask for permission.” Just how serious and at what scale are these copyright infringements you’ve observed?

For several years now, ICMP has been gathering detailed evidence of extensive copyright infringement by a number of tech companies. It’s important that when people think AI, they recall the incumbent big tech companies are as immersed, if not more so, in willful and knowing copyright infringement for AI purposes as the emerging AI specific companies.

The evidence ICMP has collated demonstrates clear breaches of legal rights and commercial duties by companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and several of its big ticket corporate divisions and services, Amazon, Adobe, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Suno, Udio and DeepSeek.

This evidence is as blatant in its clarity as it is essentially wholescale in its effects. There is barely a songwriter, composers or music company unaffected.

We have been using this detailed evidence with governments around the world in private as a principal means of showing that these companies are engaged in stream-ripping on a scale previously unseen. This unlicensed accessing of the world’s digital music is not only illegal, but the source of a panoply of downstream harms, including illegal model training, dataset commercialization and GenAI, circumvention of Technical Protection Measures, streaming fraud and other digital market impacts.

These need to be tackled as far upstream as possible, at source. There needs to be a combination of responses, including legislative, litigative, licensing, metadata and technology adoption to filter out infringements or facilitate licensed usage.

The evidence book has helped persuade a large number of governments around the world not to introduce new laws providing a free pass for AI and tech. It’s also refocusing their attention on what should really be done, and that is enforcing their laws against unlicensed use of music.

The work, alongside out member companies’ business approach, has torpedoed the longstanding and deliberately dissembling claim by some that these are binary issues of the tech sector or music. Rather, it’s a case of some companies in the tech sector don’t want to play by the rules and secure the relevant licenses first. It’s those who we are going after.

There is simply no legal or commercial barrier to training an AI model on the world’s music. See ElevenLabs as a case in point of doing things the right way by seeking permission first on an opt in basis.

The company now valued north of $22 billion. So it’s the commercial hypocrisy of the bad actors who need to be tackled. We’re working to ensure Australia’s government becomes one of dozens of others who now understand the actions and motives of Sam Altman (CEO of OpenAI), Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic) and similar.

The music community has suggested that Big AI is attempting to strong-arm governments, and that, under the right conditions, could pull off the largest copyright larceny in history. Is that hyperbole?

At ICMP we talk of four basic links in the AI market chain: accessing works, often at vast scale; the pre-training and training phase; the dataset commercialization phase and the GenAI output. Some companies enact all in-house, some outsource some phases.

Each phase implies different copyrights. And any phase engaged in with digital music without prior clearance from relevant rightholders is an infringement.

We’re seeing evidence of many of these phases across all the companies I’ve put on the record here, and several others. In response, our industry is taking the four-pronged response I mentioned — first get to governments worldwide, litigate as needed, license where wanted, adopt the right tech across all.

What we see in terms of the scale of the ingestion is simply unprecedented.

In a recent meeting with the Australian government we were able to show, at speed, all 10 of the prime minister’s favorite songs were illegally used, that all 12 Australian orchestras’ had their work infringed and that specific songs of established and emerging Australian stars were being impacted by bad actors. The fact this can be shown against such an amount of the world’s music is showing that there can be no legitimizing of these processes.

We need to refuse OpenAI, Anthropic and Big Tech’s asks and instead focus on enforcement.

Lots of political horse trading and behind-the-scenes jousting. The Australian Standing Committee on AI has put its cards on the table by calling for copyright reform in the name of AI. ICMP has replied to the PM Office’s headline ask of “what does good transparency look like regarding AI markets?”

Australian rightholders, spearheaded by our Australasian industry group AMPAL on behalf of every last Australian music publishing and production music company, are working superbly. Key senators are engaged. The tech companies are throwing the kitchen sink at this one.

Summer recess kicks in end of November. That will be a big junction but not the end of the road. The timeline will likely extend. But the targets are as clear as they are crucial.

#636. Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday

Nationwide protests led by young people were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports about looting and rioting in the evening, especially in Frankfurt, overshadowed the spirit of the demonstrations.

This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31 and November 1, 2026.

The Gen Z protests in Germany were mostly peaceful throughout the day, with tens of thousands of people having participated across big and smaller cities.

The peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by reports about violence in some cities like Frankfurt (see below).

Hesse's state interior minister said he suspects that about 100 left-wing extremists instigated the violence in Frankurt.

There were instances of disturbances in Cologne, Hamburg and Bremen, too.

Riots, looting and attacks on police broke out in several German cities after protests by tens of thousands of young people across the country demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice.

The demonstrations had been largely peaceful during the day.

But serious disturbances erupted in the evening in several places.

Clashes broke out in Cologne on Saturday, with about 200 people involved in disturbances near Cologne Cathedral.

Police officers were attacked on the square outside the famous cathedral, with bottles and bicycles hurled toward them.

In a nearby side street, a window was smashed by an electric scooter thrown during the unrest, police said.

According to regional broadcaster WDR, other groups besides Gen Z demonstrators were involved in riots.

Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was deeply saddening that peaceful protests were overshadowed by "extremists who had nothing but violence in mind."

While Gen Z protests across Germany were largely peaceful during the day, clashes were reported in several cities as night fell.

German police sealed off a major shopping street in central Frankfurt on Saturday night after rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores and attacked officers following a demonstration.

Police closed Die Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, to incoming visitors and urged bystanders to leave the area.

"Anyone not involved who is still on the Zeil can leave. Access to the Zeil is no longer possible," Frankfurt police said in a post on X and in loudspeaker announcements.

Chaotic scenes unfolded along the shopping street, where dpa journalists witnessed people breaking into stores and stealing trainers and other goods.

A specialist firearms shop was also targeted, prompting several arrests, a police spokesman said.

Police also reported attacks on officers, including attacks involving incendiary devices.

The violence erupted after police broke up a demonstration organized as part of the nationwide "Gen Z regelt" (roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge") protests.

A large contingent of officers was deployed around the Zeil, with authorities advising people to avoid the area or leave central Frankfurt.

The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.

The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.

For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.

After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."

"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.

While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."

Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.

"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.

German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.

In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.

Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.

Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.

In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.

Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.

"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.

"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.

"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."

Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said

Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.

German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.

Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.

The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).

Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.

Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.

Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.

But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.

In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.

They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.

Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.

Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.

One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.

The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.

Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig,  Nuremberg, and elsehwere.

Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.

Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.

Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.

Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.

In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.

Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.

Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.

Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.

She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.

This rainbow-hued rocky plain looks like the landscape of an alien world. And, it turns out, it is.

In this image, we can see an ancient, rocky hill on Mars. In the Red Planet's Southern Highlands, this alien terrain is chock-full of minerals, which we can see clearly defined in this color-enhanced view of the region.

This image was snapped by the HiRISE camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), which has been studying the planet's surface, atmosphere and climate since arriving in Martian orbit in March 2006.

But this isn't exactly what the surface of the planet would look like through our eyes; the image is color-enhanced. Why would scientists take a natural-color image and turn it rainbow? Doing so enhances the slight color differences in these rocks, allowing researchers to pick out the different minerals.

As pointed to above, enhancing colors in scientific images can be an incredibly useful tool for exploration.

For instance, in this image, the blue- and green-toned rocks could be full of minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, according to scientists analyzing the image. And they think that the yellow, orange and red patches may contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water.

By exploring the mineral content of rocks like this, researchers can peel back the layers of history within the Martian bedrock. The discovery of certain minerals, for example, can show that water flowed on Mars long ago, pointing to potentially habitable conditions.

So, as we can see, this striking rainbow image isn't just a beautiful landscape; it's also hiding serious clues to Mars' history.
