#574. ‘Godzilla,’ Record Anime Boom and a Global Co-Production Hunt: Takeaways From the Tokyo Film Festival and Market

The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival wrapped this week, a few days after its content market TIFFCOM, with Japan’s government talking up a JPY20 trillion ($126.6 billion) content export target, and the anime industry arriving with numbers to back it up.

The festival ran Oct. 26–Nov. 4, with TIFFCOM held Oct. 28–30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho. Across both, the talk kept returning to who owns Japanese IP, who pays to develop it and how far producers will travel to find partners. Here are the key takeaways. Related Stories John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,' Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical 'Romance & Cigarettes' and the Knicks Championship Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE)

The hardest number of the week came from the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA). Spending on Japanese anime worldwide reached a record JPY4.45 trillion ($28.2 billion) in 2025, up 15.8% on the year, according to preliminary figures presented at TIFFCOM by Hasegawa Masahiro, editor-in-chief of the AJA’s annual “Anime Industry Report.”

Much of the growth came from home. Local growth jumped to 14.1% from 4.6% in 2024, reaching JPY1.91 trillion ($12.1 billion). Overseas revenue rose 17.2% to JPY2.54 trillion ($16.1 billion), slower than the 26% of a year earlier, though overseas still accounts for 57.1% of the total.

Studio revenue also hit a record, rising 8.4% to JPY505.5 billion ($3.2 billion).

“The idea of studios holding the rights to their own works and managing them to generate revenue is growing year by year,” Hasegawa said.

The industry is also building its own institutions. The AJA named its new national prize the Nippon Anime Awards and set the first ceremony for Nov. 21, 2027, at SGC Hall Ariake in Tokyo. The name was revealed at Tokyo Anime Next, an event co-organized by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. A TIFFCOM symposium on Oct. 30 examined what the awards are for.

Japanese IP Continues to be the Market’s Currency

TIFFCOM spent three days selling Japanese stories to the world, and the Cannes Film Market signed up for more. On Oct. 29 the two markets said they would stage a second Japan IP Market in Cannes on May 14–15, 2027, following a first edition in May, when Japan was Country of Honor at the Cannes market.

Back in Tokyo, eight rights holders pitched titles in English at the Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake on the market’s first day. Shochiku offered its long-running “Otoko wa Tsurai yo” film series, Takara Tomy pitched its “Beyblade” toy franchise and Toei put forward the film “Inugamimura.”

The platforms are spending. Buddy Marini, head of Amazon MGM Studios Japan, said at a TIFFCOM session on the global potential of Japanese IP that the studio is doubling its investment to bring its content up to global standards. He shared the stage with “Kokuho” producer Matsuhashi Shinzo and “One Piece” executive producer Steven Maeda.

TIFFCOM CEO Shiina Yasushi wants Japanese companies to hold on to their IP and their overseas distribution, Hollywood style. “I believe anime is leading the way worldwide, with live-action following in its footsteps,” he told Variety ahead of the market. He plans to grow TIFFCOM well beyond its current size, venue included, by around 2030.

The buyers turned up. Registered visitors, the buyers, producers and investors who do the deals, rose 13% to 1,425, according to TIFFCOM’s preliminary figures. Those from overseas rose 9% to 814, with the North American contingent growing by a third and the European one by nearly 70%, while visitors from Japan grew 20%. Overall participation slipped to 4,405 from 4,610, mainly because fewer people came from Greater China, but the market drew participants from 51 countries and regions, up from 46. It had 317 exhibitors, against 322 last year, and its conferences and events logged around 3,000 attendances.

Big Government Targets, Struggling Filmmakers

The government set its sights high at the opening ceremony, where Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Akazawa Ryosei and Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, appearing by video, restated the goal of JPY20 trillion in overseas content sales by 2033. A Cabinet Office task force, which first met on Oct. 22, is working toward a single body to bring the government’s scattered content support under one roof.

International producers want the existing tools fixed first. At the Motion Picture Association’s annual seminar, “Tokyo Vice” producer Alex Boden said the IP360 incentive’s minimum spend, now JPY800 million ($5.1 million), shuts out independent films and co-productions, since most Japanese films cost between $1.5 million and $3 million.

“So how does a producer know that they can count on the Japan incentive in advance? That’s the question, and we need a solution,” Boden said.

Netflix production policy director Deb Richards said a lower incentive would be fine as long as it was certain and its criteria were clear. “And that’s one of the things that for the Japan incentive, the criteria is not clear,” she said.

The view from the director’s chair was bleaker. O Mipo shared this year’s Kurosawa Akira Award with Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof and spoke to Variety before the ceremony.

“I honestly don’t think there are any directors in Japan right now who are making a living solely from directing movies. They have to do other things – like streaming, TV dramas, commercials, and all sorts of other work – because you really can’t survive just from movies,” O said.

She counts herself among them. Her commercial work has dried up because a film “takes up a huger chunk of your time,” she said, and “things have gotten a bit bleak since I’m relying solely on movies.” In Japan, she added, “the reality is that you don’t get a single yen at the planning stage.”

Festival programming director Ichiyama Shozo said Japan has a surprisingly large number of talented filmmakers. “While support for Japanese cinema has increased in various forms over the past few years, support for low-budget films is still insufficient,” he told Variety.

The festival is trying to help. This year it launched TIFF Work-in-Progress for Japanese films that need money to finish production, and turned its Nippon Cinema Now section into a competition with two new awards. Tanaka Miki’s debut “Silver Express” won its best film prize.

Actor Isomura Hayato, the “Alice in Borderland” star who headed the jury for the festival’s Ethical Film Award, said Japan needs more government funding and support for entertainment and film, and pointed to South Korea, where a change of government shifted the climate for the industry.

Co-Production Partners From Well Outside Asia

The search for partners stretched well beyond the region. One producer said the subject came up a lot across TIFFCOM’s panels.

“I can tell that they’re looking for co-producers and co-producers who are technically outside of Japan or the Asian market,” he said. Panelists, he added, raised co-productions with Mongolia and the U.K. and, he believed, were looking for funding partners in South America. “That was like the main repetitive thing: looking for co-producers to help them out.”

Andrew Partridge, chief content officer at Toho Europe, said it was remarkable how similar the trends stay from year to year.

“Right now the impact of streaming investment & television commission changes worldwide remain constant here. That’s given way to the point that if traditional routes won’t fund the full whack – what will cover the tab overall? You’re seeing a real movement to emerging markets to help with that such as Africa and Middle East for example which gives rise for exciting new content mixes too,” Partridge said.

For Ervin Han, CEO and co-founder of Singapore’s Robot Playground Media, the market showed “a continued and growing interest in coproductions at both regional and international levels – understanding the dynamics, intricacies and best practices esp amongst Asian players.”

Han has seen it work. He told a TIFFCOM anime co-production panel that a meeting at the market in 2023 brought Italian co-producers to “The Violinist,” which went on to win the top prize at France’s Annecy International Animation Film Festival this year.

Even the competition jury was talking about it. Juror Alex Lo, a New York- and Tokyo-based producer whose credits include Jim Jarmusch’s Venice Golden Lion winner “Father Mother Sister Brother,” said producers in Europe, the U.S. and elsewhere “are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities,” largely because local government support is lacking.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market put that into practice. Its seventh edition selected 24 projects and partnered for the first time with Frontières, the genre co-production market of Canada’s Fantasia International Film Festival. Taiwan’s “Uncle,” from director Yen Hao-hsuan, won both the Tokyo Project Award and the Asian Gen-Z Award. Japan-Canada genre co-production “Wild Zero Overdrive,” from director Takeuchi Tetsuro, took the White Light Post-Production Award, and Brazilian director Matias Mariani’s “Nature Boy” won the Mellow Tunes Sound Design Award. Next year, the market will open up to a wider range of genres.

Chang Chen-yu, founder of Taiwan-Japan co-production fund Daily Capital, which launched at TIFFCOM on Oct. 28, said “buyers and investors from Southeast Asian markets such as Vietnam, Singapore and Indonesia had a much stronger presence at TIFFCOM.”

“Cross-border co-production between Northeast and Southeast Asia has become central to mainstream business discussions,” he said.

Daily Capital aims to raise NT$100 million (about $3.1 million) and back at least five film, TV and animation projects over its first two years. K2 Pictures and Remow are its Japanese co-development partners, and its first investment is the 1930s-set period romance series “Love Ends in Bloom.” Vietnam, meanwhile, returned with its national film pavilion for a second year.

The money is changing shape as well as source. Chang said major international streaming platforms have become more cautious with their acquisition budgets, and that the market is no longer dominated entirely by all-rights buyouts. At TIFFCOM, distributors and independent producers were regaining negotiating power, with companies favoring minimum guarantees while keeping theatrical, TV and streaming rights separate in each territory, which stretches out revenue and adds value to IP extensions.

“This year, proposals for cross-border distribution and early-stage co-production financing have increased significantly. Asian buyers and platforms – including Japanese broadcasters, regional streaming services and international distributors – are more willing to get involved early in development to spread the risk beyond a single market,” Chang said.

Japan’s production committee system is showing more flexibility toward international collaboration, welcoming cross-border investment and new distribution models, he added.

A TIFFCOM panel on film funds showed what that can look like. K2 Pictures’ K2P Film Fund I closed in February at about JPY5 billion ($32 million) as a blind pool, with investors committing before films are chosen, and aims to back around 50 films over seven years. Five of its films have reached theaters this year. MUFG Bank is also running a feasibility study for the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry on whether completion guarantees, which help U.S. producers secure bank loans, can work in Japan. K2 Pictures CEO Kii Muneyuki said it is hard to rely on overseas box office.

The broadcasters are moving in the same direction. TBS used its TIFFCOM session to set out its partnership with Hollywood’s Legendary Entertainment and the global rollout of “Sasuke,” while Nippon TV laid out its co-production frameworks, including the drama “Merry Berry Love” with South Korea’s CJ ENM.

The AI keynote went to AGBO, the studio founded by the Russo brothers. Partner Chris Brearton and chief scientific officer Dominic Hughes set out where the technology helps and where it falls short.

Hughes said AI can judge whether a play found in an attic might be Shakespeare’s, but asked to write one of its own, “you’d have the sense that it was written by a 12-year-old.”

“If you’re struggling a little bit with a character in the third act, it can provide data,” Brearton said. “Not a solution, but data.”

The pair also talked about anime and manga, and about the chance for Japanese stories to find audiences around the world.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences sent its top brass. CEO Bill Kramer, president Lynette Howell Taylor, chief membership officer Meredith Shea and Academy Museum director and president Amy Homma came to Tokyo to set out the Oscars’ global plans, and Kramer received the festival’s Global Cinema Leadership Special Award.

The share of Academy members living outside the U.S. has grown from around 5% to 25% in a decade, Kramer said. From 2029, the ceremony will stream free on YouTube to 2.5 billion people in more than 30 languages.

Asked whether Tokyo could join the six festivals whose top prizes now qualify films for the international feature race, Kramer said: “We’re looking to expand the number of festivals that help films qualify for the International Feature Film category. That’s a process that we’re undertaking this year, so stay tuned for more information on that.”

Cate Blanchett brought the Displacement Film Fund, which she co-founded, to give its first five short films their Japan premiere. Blanchett called the Academy’s move to make exiled filmmakers eligible for the Oscars “very profound.” Two of the fund’s directors, Rasoulof and Shahrbanoo Sadat, said they had little interest in a separate category for exiles.

“I really do not like to be labeled, and even this label is displaced,” Sadat said.

Tokyo Makes the A-List and Rethinks Its Standing

The festival came into this edition with a new official label. In March, FIAPF, the international federation of film producers’ associations, replaced its four-category accreditation system with a single list and designated 17 festivals as A-list, a term the industry had long used informally. Tokyo is on it, alongside Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Toronto, Busan, Shanghai and Cairo.

Jury president Rolf de Heer, asked at the jury press conference whether the label mattered, said most people who attend festivals had always considered Tokyo one of them. “Tokyo was effectively an A festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference,” he said.

The festival itself is taking stock. Festival director Hisamatsu Takeo said Tokyo will review this edition and reassess its place in Asia and globally before its 40th anniversary next year.

“I believe the direction we establish through that process will also help define TIFF’s course for the next decade, leading up to its 50th edition,” Hisamatsu told Variety.

“We are somehow in a competitive relationship with the Busan IFF, we’re close geographically and our dates are close too,” he said.

The 39th edition grew to 204 films from 184 last year and leaned on big titles. Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” opened the festival, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the first Japanese film certified as Filmed for Imax, was the centerpiece ahead of its Nov. 3 release in Japan, and Yeon Sang-ho’s “Colony” closed it. De Heer’s jury gave the Tokyo Grand Prix to Milcho Manchevski’s “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” and Narita Ryo won best actor for “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights.”

Stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami arrived at the festival’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” event two days after flying back from the film’s Los Angeles premiere at the TCL Chinese Theatre, where it drew a standing ovation.

“Feeling that raw enthusiasm firsthand made me realize all over again just how deeply Godzilla is loved around the world,” Kamiki said.

Japan was just as keen. Post its festival premiere, “Minus Zero” took JPY910 million ($5.8 million) from more than 590,000 admissions on its Nov. 3 opening day, the biggest opening day for any live-action film in Japan. That is about double the first-day figure for its predecessor, “Godzilla Minus One,” which went on to gross more than JPY7.65 billion ($50 million) at the local box office and became the first Asian production to win the visual effects Oscar.

Taiwanese director Lee Yun-chan, who recently won best director at the Busan International Film Festival, said she was struck by the rigor of the festival.

“At several festival screenings, I noticed that male audience members were also very eager to ask questions, and the audience skewed older,” Lee told Variety. One fan brought her a DVD of “The Shoe Fairy,” her film from 21 years ago, to sign.

#573. IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos

An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.

Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.

Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.

Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.

Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.

"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"

Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything

Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.

Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.

The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.

"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."

How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos

The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).

Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."

For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."

The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.

Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos

During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.

His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.

These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.

By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.

IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.

When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.

For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.

"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."

Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang

The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.

Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.

Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.

Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.

"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry.

Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites. In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite.

Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats. Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites, and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare. Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them.

"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space.

Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities.

In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.)

The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power, sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs.

"Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim."

"We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO.

"The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built."

Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available.

"We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future."

There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions."

It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement.

But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it.

Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare.

"They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative."

The plan was to defend the U.S. against Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) by using thousands of small autonomous orbiting interceptors to destroy them by collision.

"With enough investment, a lot is feasible," Bowen said. "But you're looking at many years of development and testing, solving the problem of testing kinetic weapons in space without leaving debris, and finding someone to buy the system."

It is clear from Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine that the future of warfare includes swarms of low-cost autonomous drones — and Shield Space is already planning an aggressive schedule of missions to prove that this pattern applies to the final frontier as well.

According to Ritchie, the startup hopes to quickly go from the first RPO demonstration to testing two full-sized 16U cubesats. It will then move on to a full carrier of 10 such cubesats, and then to a "super carrier" of 10 carriers, which will be deployed across multiple orbits.

"We then get towards our future vision, which we call space-based carrier strike," said Ritchie. In this scenario, "responsive launch or pre-positioned carriers will give us an ability to protect and defend entire orbits, should you choose."

Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Mark won awards two years in a row at the Aerospace Media Awards for features he had written on the history of drones and astronaut training. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

An annual tradition of amazement under the stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Students gathered under the stars in Hawaii recently to explore the awesome nature of the night sky together.

From Oct. 19 to Oct. 22, more than 1,400 students on the Big Island of Hawaii gathered for the Journey Through the Universe event to explore astronomy together.

The Journey Through the Universe program is currently in its 23rd year. It was originally developed by the National Center for Earth and Space Science Education (NCESSE) and later introduced in Hawaii by the international Gemini Observatory, a program within the U.S. National Science Foundation's NOIRLab (National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory) that works with the Department of Education Hilo-Waiākea.

The program aims to introduce students in the Hilo-Waiākea public school system to astronomy as well as the incredible science that happens across Hawaii. The students who participate range from preschoolers to seniors in high school, so the program introduces some students to astronomy and helps others explore possible careers in STEM fields.

This year, the program brought in 19 volunteer educators from scientific institutions like Maunakea Observatories and supported hands-on activities and lessons that went from the classroom to under the Milky Way.

This image shows a growing love for astronomy in progress. From the red glow of a skywatching night (red light doesn't interfere with our ability to see at night like white light does) to the scattered telescopes and students standing under the stars, this scene paints a larger picture.

This is just one program, but in bringing together volunteers, educators, scientists and students, the program has created an incredible and enduring learning experience.

Whether or not students walk away wanting to pursue a career in STEM, this incredible immersion in astronomy can help to foster a lifelong appreciation for science and nature. It's always a great idea to gather under the stars and explore together.

#569. The hidden cost of flexible work in academia: women do more parenting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Flexible working conditions often mean mothers in academia do more parenting than men. Credit: Jelena Cvetkovic/Alamy

Flexible working policies at universities that are designed to make work life easier for parents and carers can reinforce gendered parenting roles, according to a growing body of research published this year. For instance, when workplaces offer flexibility, women end up taking on a greater share of parenting than men.

Universities “have all these policies in place, and we see so many women in science,” that many people assume that women can participate in work as much as men, says Cassidy Sugimoto, an information scientist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. But “the problem is being solved with women carrying an extraordinary burden”.

Research has already established that parenthood has a greater impact on the careers of female academics than those of men. Sugimoto and her colleagues wanted to find out how much parenting academics do, and how that affects their productivity.

They surveyed more than 10,000 parent academics with academic or non-academic partners at universities and research organizations globally1. They found that women in academia were more likely to be the lead parent and do most of the parenting. Even when women shared parenting or took a secondary role, what the authors call satellite parenting, women ended up doing more than men did when they were the satellite parent. The only task that men were consistently doing more than women was coaching their child’s sports team, says survey co-author Gemma Derrick, a meta-researcher at the University of Bristol, UK.

The team then wanted to understand why women in academia were doing more parenting. Sugimoto and her colleagues found that women used flexible working policies — such as being able to adjust their hours to work earlier or later in the day — to take on more parenting responsibilities2. In academic couples, men, however, used the option of flexibility to justify why they did not do as much parenting as their female partner. For example, some men said that their partner chose to have a more flexible career to look after children.

A female academic from the United Kingdom wrote in the survey that work flexibility meant it was easy for their partner to rely on them “always being available” to help with the kids. Another academic from the United States said: “I have the flexibility to drop off, pick up kids, send them for all activities, and feed them. I have the flexibility to make up all the work time I give up during daytime at night, work till 2am or at least midnight.”

Sanjee Perera, a workforce researcher at the Adelaide University, Australia, says academia has the “illusion of flexibility” because researchers have more autonomy to fit work around parenting responsibilities. But researchers are expected to publish papers, secure external funding, supervise students, teach and attend conferences, she says. “It’s almost like an open-ended workload.”

When men in academia attempted to use flexible working to parent more, they often faced belittling comments or impacts on their careers, says Derrick. The perception of parenting as a gendered responsibility is changing over time, she says. “The question is whether it’s changing fast enough,” she adds.

Another survey3 of 26 female academics in the United Kingdom, by Guoxin Ma, a workplace equity researcher at the Royal Agricultural University in Cirencester, UK, and their colleagues reported that flexible workplace policies, such as working from home or having adjustable working hours, made it harder for women to progress their careers after having children.

Some respondents said that they were seen as less committed to work because they worked from home, finished early or were part-time, while others said that they continued working while on leave because there was no one else to do their work.

Parenting became more equal in many households during the COVID-19 pandemic, says Sugimoto. Some couples looked after their children on alternating days or in ‘shifts’, particularly if one parent had fixed working hours. Flexible working arrangements existed before the pandemic, but now ‘hybrid working’ such as online teaching and meetings has became more normalized4.

#567. NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice

Located in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, Vega Island has a particularly haunting appearance when viewed from above. Its rocky and icy features resemble a grinning skull seen from the side, seemingly gazing toward nearby Devil Island. But behind this unusual sight is a more serious story about the changing condition of Antarctica's glaciers.

NASA satellite images show the island during the beginning of Antarctic autumn and during spring. The images were captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.)

Several natural landmarks create the skull's distinctive appearance. A nunatak, which is a rocky peak rising above the surrounding ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge of material left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth. Meanwhile, Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms what looks like the skull's lower jaw.

The two satellite views also reveal a striking difference in snow coverage. In March 2025, snow blanketed the icy terrain, consistent with March being the wettest month in the region. By October 2026, however, extensive sections of the island were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the unusually large areas of exposed ice observed in October. According to Pelto, the exposed surfaces on Vega Island and neighboring islands suggest that relatively little fresh snow accumulated over the winter. Some of that snow was also lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds that swept snow away.

“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”

The lack of snow could have important consequences as Antarctica moves into its warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker, exposed ice absorbs more solar energy. As daylight increases and temperatures rise, these darker surfaces are likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up glacier melting.

Even a modest amount of new snowfall could temporarily slow that process by covering the exposed ice.

“Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said.

Continued melting could also gradually transform the island's unsettling appearance. The same ice and rock formations that give Vega Island its skull shape are vulnerable to changes as the glaciers retreat.

“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”

Scientists have been studying Vega Island's glaciers for decades, and satellite observations have played an important role in documenting their condition.

One of the earliest detailed surveys appeared in a 1982 study that used early Landsat satellite data, aerial photography, and topographic maps to examine the island's ice cover. Researchers identified four ice caps, along with rocky cliffs extending above the ice and glaciers flowing outward from the ice caps. Altogether, they documented 29 glaciers across Vega Island.

One of these, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been monitored in detail since the Antarctic summer of 1998-1999. Measurements collected over that period show an overall reduction in the glacier's mass.

The changes are not limited to Devil's Bay Glacier. Satellite observations spanning recent decades reveal that other glaciers on Vega Island have also lost ice, exposing increasing amounts of the underlying bedrock.

Long before satellites began monitoring its ice, Vega Island played an unexpected role in one of Antarctica's dramatic early exploration stories.

The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 traveled to the region to investigate the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding areas. What began as a scientific mission turned into a desperate struggle for survival.

During the expedition, the explorers became separated into three groups, each forced to endure the Antarctic winter in a different location. Their situation became even more dangerous when pack ice destroyed their ship, leaving them stranded in one of the world's most unforgiving environments.

Despite the ordeal, Vega Island eventually became the setting for a moment of hope. In spring 1903, two of the separated groups reunited at a location later named Cape Well-met, near what now resembles the “forehead” of the island's giant skull.

Not long afterward, an Argentinean expedition arrived and rescued the survivors, bringing their extraordinary Antarctic ordeal to an end.

Today, Vega Island remains a place where dramatic natural formations, a remarkable history of exploration, and the effects of a changing climate come together. Its ghostly skull may be one of Antarctica's most unusual sights, but the gradual transformation of the ice that shapes it tells an even more important story.

"It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The launch of NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026 caused significant disturbances in Earth's ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found.

The study, by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan, analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers, used by U.S. scientific institutions to measure the minuscule motions of Earth's tectonic plates in the lead-up to earthquakes. By measuring how long it takes GPS signals to travel from space to ground stations, the researchers were able to reconstruct how the passage of the Artemis II mission's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket changed the concentrations of free electrons in the ionosphere — the electrically charged layer of Earth's atmosphere at altitudes above 30 miles (50 kilometers).

The measurements found that the ionospheric disturbances resulting from the sheer power of the Artemis II launch were more significant than any caused by other rocket launches to date and up to ten times more intense than those observed following the test launches of SpaceX's Starship, which is twice as powerful as the SLS based on liftoff thrust.

Artemis II saw humans return to the lunar space for the first time in more than fifty years, a mission that NASA hopes will pave the way for lunar landings and eventually the establishment of a sustained human presence on the moon.

During the mission's launch, ground-based GPS stations detected changes in the ionospheric electron density equivalent to positioning errors of several meters. Such inaccuracies could easily throw self-driving cars off track, potentially causing traffic collisions, according to Charles Lin, an earth science professor at National Cheng Kung University and one of the co-authors of the paper.

"A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," Lin told Space.com. "It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

GPS receivers determine their position on Earth's surface at any single moment by measuring their distance to four different GPS satellites. When concentrations of free electrons in the upper atmosphere change — for example during a solar storm or after a rocket passage — the signal reaches Earth either faster or more slowly, resulting in inaccurate measurements.

Satellites of the U.S. GPS constellation and other Global Navigation Satellite Systems orbit Earth at an altitude of around 12,550 miles (20,200 kilometers), far above the upper edge of the ionosphere, meaning the positioning, navigation and timing signal these satellites transmit must pass through this volatile atmospheric layer to reach Earth.

Severe solar storms can disrupt GPS signals for days by dumping energy into the atmosphere in the form of charged particles from the sun. The impact of rocket launches, triggered by the supersonic flight of the rocket body through the high-altitude air, is much more short-lived. As the rocket soars up, it creates a shock wave, which virtually punches a hole into the ionosphere.

In the aftermath of the Artemis II launch, the researchers observed two such holes — one left behind by the 212-foot-long (65 meters) SSL core stage, and the other caused by two subsequent thruster burns of the rocket's upper stage. In both cases, these holes stretched across the American continent from East to West like giant 3,100-mile (5,000-kilometer) contrails.

Despite the enormous power of the SLS core stage, the disturbance caused by the second-stage burns directly inside the ionosphere was far more prominent.

Those two burns, at altitudes around 115 miles (185 kilometers), took place more than an hour after lift-off and allowed the Orion capsule to break free from Earth's gravity and head for the moon.

"Rocket launches from the ground to space produce that kind of effect, but we have never seen this kind of orbital maneuver in an interplanetary mission," said Lin. "In the future, as we are going to see many more missions going to the moon and to Mars, these space weather effects will become much more significant."

The study was published as a pre-print online in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

#565. Taylor Swift’s Canceled Vienna Concerts Due to Thwarted Terrorist Plot to Be Subject of Documentary

The doc will juxtapose two youth subcultures: 'the inclusive, empowered world of the Swifties and a realm of toxic masculinity, fueled by online radicalization'

In August 2024, three dates of Taylor Swift‘s epic global “Eras” tour were canceled in Vienna after authorities were warned of a terrorist plot.

The in-depth story of this planned jihadist attack — which was thwarted by Austrian authorities, thanks in part to a tip-off from U.S. intelligence — is now the subject of a high-profile doc working-titled “Taylor Swift Wien,” being co-directed by Andreas Pichler (“Tesla Files,” “The Milk System”) and Veronika Kaserer (“Hunt for the Mafia – The ‘Ndrangheta in Germany”). “Wien” is the German word for Vienna. Related Stories John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,' Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical 'Romance & Cigarettes' and the Knicks Championship Oscar Predictions: Documentary Feature — Will the Branch Embrace ‘You Can See Everything’ or Snub the Frontrunner (Again)?

“Taylor Swift Wien,” per its synopsis, will juxtapose “two vastly different youth subcultures: the inclusive, empowered world of the Swifties and a realm of toxic masculinity, fueled by online radicalization and a desperate need for validation.”

That realm prompted two male teenagers to devise a plot, using explosives and other weapons, with which they reportedly intended to kill as many Taylor Swift concert attendees as possible. The Vienna events were expected to draw more than 200,000 fans from across the world to the Austrian capital’s Ernst Happel Stadium.

Georg Tschurtschenthaler, chief creative officer at German’s Beetz Brothers — which is co-producing the doc with Austria’s Markand Media — tells Variety the doc will show the inside story of this failed terrorist attack from several points of view. One is a “ticking clock” thriller of how the secret services, including the CIA, the U.K.’s MI5, and Austria and Germany’s agencies, managed to prevent the attack.

The doc’s other principal storyline delves into the Swiftie community in Vienna. “We are following three female characters for whom, when they learn that the concert has been canceled, it was, of course, a shock,” Tschurtschenthaler said. In what becomes a female empowerment storyline, they organize psychological support for their fellow fans, getting in touch with the Austrian police and even meeting with Austrian Chancellor Karl Nehammer and members of the country’s secret services.

The third narrative element of “Taylor Swift Wien” is the main perpetrator, the then 19-year-old Austrian citizen of North Macedonian descent known only as Beran A., who had sworn allegiance to the Islamic State. He “had been kind of radicalized through TikTok,” said Tschurtschenthaler, who noted: “There is a new generation of young Islamic terrorists that is growing worldwide who are steeped in social media and different from the old terrorists trained in Al Qaeda camps.”

“Taylor Swift Wien” will therefore be a mix of genres, combining “ticking clock thriller, female empowerment of the fans and the depiction of the new Muslim manosphere” as a form of revenge against Western liberalism and feminism, Tschurtschenthaler noted. The producer said Beetz Brothers have made Swift’s management aware that this doc is being made.

The distribution plan is for “Taylor Swift Wien” to air on German broadcaster ZDF in October 2027 followed by an international rollout.

Swift cautiously waited two weeks to issue her first statement after the Vienna Aug. 8-10 concerts had been canceled, calling it “devastating” in an Aug. 21 Instagram post commemorating the end of the tour’s European leg.

“The reason for the cancellations filled me with a new sense of fear, and a tremendous amount of guilt because so many people had planned on coming to those shows,” Swift added. “But I was also so grateful to the authorities because thanks to them, we were grieving concerts and not lives,” she continued, noting: “In cases like this one, ‘silence’ is actually showing restraint, and waiting to express yourself at a time when it’s right to.”

"It was like looking for a needle in a haystack."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping.

That means that Olympus Mons, the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system, may in fact be a slumbering giant.

The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area.

TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism.

Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack."

Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected.

The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.

The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism.

"It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said.

The team thinks that these gases have been rising from the interior of Mars during the Martian winter, becoming blocked by ice. When this ice sublimates, changes directly from solid to gas, during summer, the gas is released, prompting spikes in hydrogen chloride seen by the TGO.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," said Mège. "A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. "We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food."

Mège and colleagues theorize that the gas is connected to "volcanic plumbing" in the form of a dormant magma chamber under the surface of Mars.

Regions like this could become hotspots (pun not intended) in the search for life on Mars. That is because magmatic gases like hydrogen chloride would have been more abundant in the past, creating a thicker Martian atmosphere and warmer climate.

Not only would this have led to liquid water covering much of the Martian surface, but when lava bubbled through the Martian crust and met groundwater, warm habitable niches ideal for microbial life could have been forged.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," Mège concluded.

The team's research was published in the journal Science Advances on Wednesday (Nov. 4).

#563. A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials

Scientists at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory have discovered that applying a small amount of pressure can dramatically alter the magnetic properties of a promising new class of materials called altermagnets. Using neutron experiments, the researchers uncovered how a simple mechanical squeeze can change the way these materials behave, offering a potential new approach to controlling magnetism.

The results, reported in two consecutive studies published in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, show that mechanical strain can influence both magnetic structures and the movement of electrons. This ability could provide a straightforward way to control materials being investigated for advanced electronic technologies.

Why Altermagnets Matter for Future Electronics

One particularly promising application involves spintronics, short for spin electronics. Unlike conventional electronics, which processes and stores information using the electrical charge of electrons, spintronics also takes advantage of a property known as electron spin.

If scientists can identify and develop suitable materials, including altermagnets, this approach could lead to major advances in technologies ranging from wireless communication to quantum computing.

"By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies," said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

A Simple Squeeze Reveals Surprising Magnetic Changes

To investigate how pressure affects these materials, the ORNL team placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between a pair of titanium plates and gently compressed them.

Using neutron diffraction at ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source, the scientists examined what happened to the magnetic structures inside the crystals. They found that the applied pressure changed the relative populations of magnetic domains, which are regions within a material that have particular magnetic arrangements. The strain also altered an electrical phenomenon called the anomalous Hall effect, providing evidence that the mechanical squeeze influenced the materials' electrical behavior.

"What's exciting is that one creative experimental idea -- a small mechanical squeeze between two plates -- can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism," said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author on both linked publications.

The findings highlight how a relatively simple experiment can uncover new ways to manipulate magnetic materials, potentially helping researchers develop the building blocks for future spintronic devices.

ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source is a DOE Office of Science user facility.

Tim Burton is bringing Halloween Town to the luxury fashion world.

Loewe has teamed up with the filmmaker and Disney for a new capsule collection inspired by the 1993 stop-motion classic “The Nightmare Before Christmas,” marking the Spanish fashion house’s latest foray into Hollywood-inspired fashion. The collection, launching Nov. 12, will span handbags, ready-to-wear, leather goods, accessories and scented candles. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Animated Feature — A New and Competitive Era for the Medium That Isn't Just for Kids ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories

Among the pieces teased ahead of the launch are a handbag featuring a Jack Skellington illustration hidden in its lining, a crocheted Wolfman keychain and a woven black-and-orange leather bucket bag adorned with protruding snakes. Other designs take inspiration from the film’s eccentric cast of characters, including Zero and the Harlequin Demon.

The collaboration brings together Burton and Loewe creative directors Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, who took the reins at the LVMH-owned label in 2025. The partnership draws on the shared emphasis on craftsmanship between the fashion house and Burton’s approach to filmmaking, particularly the handmade puppets, sets and intricate animation that brought “The Nightmare Before Christmas” to life.

“I love [stop motion] because it’s all handmade,” Burton told Vanity Fair in an interview accompanying the announcement. “When you see the puppets and the sets, you wish everybody could experience the tactile nature of what goes into making a stop-motion film, or any film.”

The filmmaker also reflected on how the rise of artificial intelligence has deepened his appreciation for the human element of artistic creation. “The more [AI] keeps going that way, the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.”

Although closely associated with Burton, “The Nightmare Before Christmas” was directed by Henry Selick and based on an original poem by Burton, who also produced the film. Released by Disney’s Touchstone Pictures banner in 1993, the musical fantasy follows Jack Skellington, the Pumpkin King of Halloween Town, as he attempts to take over Christmas.

The release continues Loewe’s longstanding relationship with the entertainment industry, particularly its collaborations with beloved animated films. Under former creative director Jonathan Anderson, the house partnered with Japan’s Studio Ghibli on three collections inspired by “My Neighbor Totoro” in 2021, “Spirited Away” in 2022 and “Howl’s Moving Castle” in 2023.

The label’s Hollywood connections also extend to the screen. Anderson, during his tenure at Loewe, developed a close creative partnership with director Luca Guadagnino, designing costumes for the filmmaker’s 2024 releases “Challengers,” starring Zendaya, and “Queer,” starring Daniel Craig. Loewe also enlisted Guadagnino to direct a short film for its Spring/Summer 2024 campaign.

The Loewe x Disney Tim Burton’s “The Nightmare Before Christmas” collection launches Nov. 12.

Swift had a pretty good 22-year run, but NASA wanted the scope to keep going even longer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road.

Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit.

The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell, who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.

Several videos circulating on social media appear to show the spacecraft's fiery reentry, though it has yet to be independently verified.

Likely reentry of @NASA's #Swift observatory over Sumatra & Malaysia at 12:39 UTC today.November 4, 2026

Likely reentry of @NASA's #Swift observatory over Sumatra & Malaysia at 12:39 UTC today.November 4, 2026

Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe. "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility.

"Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement. "This typically took Swift about a minute to do."

Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system.

And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20. (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.)

"Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement.

"In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added.

Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out.

In September 2025, NASA awarded the Arizona company Katalyst Space a $30 million contract to design, launch and operate a robotic spacecraft that would meet up with Swift and boost it to a higher orbit, thus extending its operational life.

Swift was falling back to Earth: It had no onboard thrusters to counteract the effect of atmospheric drag, which had been pulling the observatory down ever since it launched. The process was accelerating as Swift got lower, so Katalyst had to work fast. And the company did: It launched its refrigerator-sized, three-armed LINK servicing spacecraft on July 3, targeting an August capture of Swift.

That didn't happen, however. LINK suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which nixed the planned meetup. Still, it was a worthwhile effort, according to NASA.

"From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25, the day that LINK itself crashed back to Earth.

"And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit," he added.

Swift's crash today wasn't exactly unusual, by the way. At least three large objects — dead satellites or spent rocket bodies — fall back to Earth every day on average, a 2025 report found. And that number is bound to rise in the coming years, as humanity builds out more and more megaconstellations in Earth orbit.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 5 at 4:45 a.m. EST (0944 GMT) to include social media videos that may show the spacecraft's fiery demise.

#560. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].
