How "Forrest Gump", pizza, and a massive supporting cast of furballs came together to make one of "Star Trek"'s finest hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history, but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment.

Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

But it was "DS9"'s "Trials and Tribble-ations" that turned out to be the more memorable voyage to "Trek" past, as Captain Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) — with the help of some then-state-of-the-art digital trickery — came face-to-face with a young Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner).

While "Flashback" aired within days of "Trek"'s September 8 birthday, fans had to wait a little longer for "DS9"'s contribution to the celebrations. Showrunner Ira Steven Behr was keen to avoid disrupting the space station-set drama's story arc for a comedic diversion, meaning that "Trials and Tribble-ations" didn't debut until November 4, 1996.

In the wake of "Flashback" — not to mention Spock and Scotty's comebacks in "The Next Generation" stories "Unification" and "Relics" — the "DS9" writers' room had already decided they needed to take a very different approach.

Early on, "Battlestar Galactica" creator Ronald D. Moore pitched a follow-up to Original Series episode "A Piece of the Action" (aka the one where the residents of Iotia brought 1920s gangsters to life). In an extremely meta concept that predated "Galaxy Quest" by three years, the story would have taken the Enterprise crew to a planet of Kirk and Spock impersonators.

"For the thirtieth anniversary, you go back, and you're basically going back to the planet of 'Star Trek' fans," Moore recalled in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross. "They have conventions; they know all the adventures. It's a phenomenon, and you could comment on 'Star Trek' as a whole. I thought it would be interesting. But [fellow writer] René Echevarria thought it was a dangerous show to do, that we would be talking down to the fans on some level, and perhaps it wasn't the best way to go."

Instead, Echevarria suggested telling a story in the vein of Woody Allen's "Zelig" or "Forrest Gump" (then a zeitgeisty, multi-Oscar-winning box-office smash) and integrating the "Deep Space Nine" crew with the events of an Original Series episode.

"I thought, 'What bigger treat could there be than to go back into the past and board the original Enterprise and have a mission there?'" Echevarria said in a 1996 making-of documentary. "And Ron immediately said, 'It's gotta be "The Trouble with Tribbles!"'"

"The Trouble with Tribbles", a 1967 episode from "Star Trek"'s second season, is one of the most famous in the franchise's history. As well as featuring some minor scuffles with Klingons, it sees the Enterprise and Deep Space Station K-7 infested with the eponymous tribbles — cute, cuddly furballs of calm that reproduce at a dangerously exponential rate.

In "Trials and Tribble-ations", a timey-wimey incident involving the Bajoran Orb of Time transports the USS Defiant (one of the best "Star Trek" spaceships) back to the era of Kirk and Spock's famous five-year mission.

As Sisko recounts the adventure to a pair of agents from Starfleet's Department of Temporal Investigations (named Dulmur and Lucsly in homage to "The X-Files"), we learn how he, Dax (Terry Farrell), O'Brien (Colm Meaney), and Bashir (Alexander Siddig) spent a day playing Original Series cosplay on Kirk's Enterprise. It's "Star Trek"'s answer to "Back to the Future: Part II", as the crew interacts with established events while taking pains not to mess with history.

Although most of the guest stars from "The Trouble with Tribbles" had passed away over the intervening decades, one actor who'd played a pivotal role was still around. By the time he turned up in "Star Trek", 20-something stand-up comedian Charlie Brill had already brushed shoulders with pop-culture legend, having shared the bill with the Beatles when they made their famous appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in February 1964.

Three years later he'd swapped Lennon and McCartney for Kirk and Spock, playing a Klingon spy masquerading as human Arne Darvin, whose cover is ultimately blown by the famously Klingon-phobic tribbles. In the newer episode, the older Darvin travels back in time to assassinate Kirk, plotting his revenge with a bomb implanted in an unfortunate tribble. Thwarting the evil scheme — and preserving the timeline — forms the basis of Sisko's mission.

Brill's return was seemingly written in the stars. When planning the episode, Behr and the other writers met for lunch at Mulberry Street Pizza in Beverly Hills and noted that the actor was alive and still working in the business. Then, just as they were talking about him, they happened to spot Brill across the very same restaurant.

"What were the chances that we would be talking about this old TV episode from 30 years ago, and the guy who we were talking about to bring back on the show would be standing there ordering a slice of pizza?" Behr recalled at the Trek Talks telethon (via TrekMovie).

But however strong its story, "Trials and Tribble-ations" was always going to live and die by its recreation of ' 60s-era "Trek". The production team subsequently pulled out all the stops, with Behr suggesting at the time that it may have been the most expensive hour of TV ever made.

The actors were kitted out in era-appropriate primary-colored outfits and given '60s hairdos. The make-up team also recreated the appearance of the Original Series' Klingons, whose very different look — "We do not discuss it with outsiders," says Worf — would later be explained away in a "Star Trek: Enterprise" two-parter.

The late Walter Koenig (who'd featured as Chekov in "The Trouble with Tribbles") showed the younger officers how to flip open a communicator, and the stunt team choreographed fights to look like the cheesy, Western-inspired brawls of a bygone era.

Behind the scenes, production designer Michael Okuda and his team used a mixture of original plans and scans of the episodes to painstakingly recreate the sets, while the visual effects team constructed an exact half-scale replica of the original 11-foot Enterprise shooting model housed in the Smithsonian.

The biggest magic trick, however, was dependent on CG technology — then very much in its infancy — making everyone believe that Sisko and co were walking the same corridors as Kirk. VFX supervisor Gary Hutzel had provided proof-of-concept early in the process:

"He showed us a clip from the old show," said Behr. "We looked at it and said, 'Okay, that looks good, but what does that have to do with us?' And he said, 'Well, you see that guy coming in through the door? That's not from the 1967 episode. That's one of our people!'"

Shooting in front of blue- and green-screens, the actors' performances were meticulously matched to the Original Series episode. Early on, Moore had identified two sequences from "The Trouble with Tribbles" that would be perfect for selling the concept: Kirk dressing down a line-up of officers after a bar room brawl and Tribbles raining down on Kirk from a storage container.

O'Brien and Bashir were digitally pasted over the original actors in the former, while the latter was explained away by Sisko and Dax's madcap dash to find the elusive explosive tribble. In most other shots, the DS9ers became background observers in existing scenes.

But there were still debates to be had over whether the two captains should meet. "It led to one of the most vociferous arguments we've had," said Behr, a passionate advocate for the "yes" camp. "We were so deadlocked, and there was so much emotion in the air, we actually turned to the writer intern and said, ‘What do you think?’ End of stalemate. Of course, being an intern and being a smart guy, he sided with his executive producer. And life went on." (The scene in which Sisko hands Kirk a duty roster for approval was actually lifted from another Original Series episode, "Mirror, Mirror", with Brooks replacing Barbara Luna (Lt. Marlena Moreau) on the bridge.)

It was all worth the effort. "Trials and Tribble-ations" was the most-watched episode of "DS9"'s fifth season, bagged nominations for three Emmys and a Hugo, and is now widely regarded as one of the best "Trek" episodes of all time.

David Gerrold, who wrote "The Trouble with Tribbles" and appeared as an extra in "Trials and Tribble-ations", described it as "possibly the best episode of 'Star Trek' after the Original Series," and various members of the writers' room have described it as a highlight of their time on the final frontier.

"From the writers to the director to the lighting, costumes, the set, sound effects, visual effects — everybody really put in so much time on that episode to really recreate the original Enterprise in any way they possibly could," said Moore. "Everybody was staring at film clips, doing research into [prop/costume] materials. It was a mania, and everybody just threw themselves into it. They wanted to make it great. And it shows."

'The Trouble with Tribbles' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' are available to stream on Paramount+ in both the US and UK.

After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. #557. Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

#556. Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.

Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.

Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production

The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.

Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.

#555. Clio Barnard’s ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’ Bought by Kino Lorber for North America (EXCLUSIVE)

The film — starring Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Jay Lycurgo, Daryl McCormack and Lola Petticrew — won the audience award in Cannes' Directors' Fortnight competition.

Fresh from landing eight nominations from the British Independent Film Awards earlier this week, Clio Barnard’s critically acclaimed “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” has landed theatrical distribution in the U.S.

Kino Lorber has acquired North American distribution rights to the film, starring fast-rising U.K. and Irish actors Anthony Boyle (“Manhunt”), Joe Cole (“Gangs of London,” “Peaky Blinders”), Jay Lycurgo(“Steve”), Daryl McCormack (“Wake Up Dead Man,” “Bad Sisters”), and Lola Petticrew (“Furious”). Related Stories Pedro Pascal on Learning Cello for ‘Behemoth!,’ Why ‘You’ve Got to Eat S---’ to Make It in Hollywood and the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Line His Character Says 'The Odyssey' Oscar Blitz to Begin With Robert Downey Jr., Guillermo del Toro and Steven Spielberg as Moderators

Based on the novel by Keiran Goddard and adapted by Irish playwright and screenwriter EndaWalsh (“Die My Love,” “Small Things Like These”), “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” had its world premiere in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight, where it won the people’s choice audience award. It recently screened at the Rome Film Festival, where it landed the top prize in the progressive cinema competition and Boyle shared the best actor prize. At the recently-announced BIFA nominations, its nod included best British independent film, best director, best screenplay and best ensemble performance.

Kino Lorber is planning a 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital, educational, and home video release.

“I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” follows childhood friends Patrick, Shiv, Rian, Oli, and Conor, who grew up on a Birmingham estate, where they skipped school together and dreamt of the lives they would have one day. But now that they’ve hit thirty, a harsher reality has set in, and those dreams haven’t materialised quite how they imagined. Patrick (Boyle) and Shiv (Petticrew) are still madly in love andhappily married, but their relationship is rocked when an old secret opens up new wounds. Charismatic Oli (Lycurgo), always the life and soul of the group, is partying too hard and is fading by the day. Conor (McCormack) has a baby on the way and a business plan that could change everything. Only Rian (Cole) has left the estate, moving to London for a high paying job in property development, but is lonely and disconnected, missing home and his family of close friends. As they fight for their futures, rifts start to form in their once unbreakable friendships, and the dreams they once shared seem more out of reach than ever.

“When I read Keiran’s novel ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’ I absolutely loved being in thecompany of Shiv, Patrick, Conor, Oli and Rian. I wanted to share this wonderful friendship groupand the story of the struggles faced by their generation with cinema audiences so I’m absolutelythrilled that the film will have a release in the USA,” said Barnard, for whom the film marks her fifth feature as director. Barnard’s previous feature “Ali & Ava” also premiered in the Directors’ Fortnight in Cannes and would win two BIFAs and be nominated for two BAFTAs.

The deal for “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” was negotiated by Kino Lorber VP of acquisitionsKaroliina Dwyer with Charades and Gersh.

“Director Clio Barnard has crafted something truly special with ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,’a beautifully observed coming of age story that sensitively captures a generation grappling withunrealized dreams,” said Dwyer. ”Her superb cast brings warmth and vulnerability to the fivefriends at the heart of the film, with an infectious energy that sweeps you into their sharedcelebrations, fears, and heartbreaks. We’re thrilled to bring this stunning film to North Americanaudiences.”

The MCU’s Multiverse Saga is nearly over, but there are plenty more Marvel movies and shows on the horizon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Marvel fatigue? Think again, especially after Spider-Man: Brand New Day made over $2.5 billion worldwide and Avengers: Doomsday is looking hot, hot, hot!

But even after the uneven Multiverse Saga ends (hopefully on a high note), Marvel Studios won’t be stopping. So, we've put together a list of all the upcoming MCU movies and shows confirmed so far.

While the MCU isn't stopping, Marvel has slowed its roll, with the powers that be returning to the “quality over quantity” approach that defined Marvel Studios’ Infinity Saga output. This means no more than three movies per year and, perhaps more importantly, severely cutting down on TV productions, with a focus on multi-season shows rather than limited series that should’ve been a movie.

It’s a time of change for both Disney and Marvel, but it seems everyone agrees the big screen reigns supreme, so expect a thinner streaming output and more relevant movies starring characters you actually know.

More will be revealed in due time, but for now, here’s what lies at the Multiverse Saga’s end and beyond...

Spoilers ahead for the Marvel Cinematic Universe so far.

Watch Marvel movies and shows on Disney+:Disney+ (With Ads): $11.99/monthDisney+ Premium (No Ads): $18.99/month or $189.99/year

Release date: December 18, 2026 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr.

Earth’s Mightiest Heroes (from different Earths, actually) are assembling again in December 2026.

Avengers: Doomsday's cast looks ridiculously stacked, and it’ll finally realize the dream of bringing together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, and the X-Men (Fox’s original ones, that is) on the big screen. It’s a lot to absorb, and we don’t really know what's going on, but the trailers released so far are promising.

Anthony & Joe Russo (Captain America: The Winter Soldier & Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War & Endgame) are returning to direct, so that’s a good reason to be hyped even if the duo’s post-Marvel career hasn’t been the most exciting. Stephen McFeely (one of their two go-to scribes) is also back, and Michael Waldron (Loki) is helping out as well. It’s an all-star team for the most ambitious MCU project to date, at least until it all culminates in...

Release window: March 2027 | Showrunner: Dario Scardapane | Cast: Charlie Cox, Mike Colter, Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter

Daredevil: Born Again’s debut season was far from perfect, but most viewers agreed that Season 2 was a marked improvement.

Hopefully, that energy will continue in the third and final outing, as the Defenders reunite, with Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter, and Mike Colter all returning from their Netflix shows. Another shocker is the (unofficially) confirmed return of Elodie Yung’s Elektra.

We suspect some of these characters will be transferred to movies post-Secret Wars. In any case, Born Again’s final season should be packed, especially if Marvel Television is sticking to eight or nine episodes.

Release date: December 17, 2027 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr.

Practically nothing about the follow-up to Avengers: Doomsday has been revealed yet (though we assume the MCU’s main players will be part of the ensemble), but we know it fully starts shooting in late 2026 and is eyeing a Christmas 2027 arrival. The plan is to leave a year-long wait between the two event movies, leaving fans hanging like back in the MCU’s glory days.

The title comes from Jonathan Hickman’s Secret Wars (2015), which is probably the main source of inspiration for the upcoming big-screen event. Incursions (realities bleeding into each other) have already been set up during the Multiverse Saga, and we know Doomsday directly deals with the multiverse’s breaking point, so it’s easy to see where the larger picture is going.

No spoilers here, but prepare for a very different kind of Avengers flick if Battleworld is indeed the main setting.

Release date: May 5, 2028 | Director: Jake Schreier | Cast: Kit Connor, Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Christopher Abbott

Whatever happens in Secret Wars (we’ve heard Marvel Studios intends to soft-reboot), Phase Seven of the MCU will kick off with a long-awaited, fresh take on the X-Men — now part of the larger Marvel universe housing all characters. Thunderbolts* director Jake Schreier will be directing, with the same writing team from that movie joining him for another Marvel adventure.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day already did some heavy lifting when it came to setting up one of its leads (Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey), but it’s unclear how the whole group will be assembled.

We know for sure Cyclops (Kit Connor), Rogue (Inde Navarrette), Emma Frost (Samara Weaving), Storm (Maya Boyd), Angel (Asa Germann), Charles Xavier (Christopher Abbott), and Mr. Sinister (Adam Driver) are confirmed to appear, but the cast should grow in the coming months.

Release date: July 28, 2028 | Director: Shawn Levy | Cast: Ryan Gosling (more to be confirmed)

Phase Seven’s second movie will be an unexpected one, but the fan reaction to its reveal was glowing: Ghost Rider, starring Ryan Gosling, with Deadpool & Wolverine’s Shawn Levy directing.

The duo worked together on Star Wars: Starfighter, and it seems it went so well that Disney and Marvel are happy with them reviving the Spirit of Vengeance as the MCU expands its dark borders.

It’s too early to even know which Ghost Rider that Gosling will be playing (Johnny Blaze or Danny Ketch) or where the plot is going, but considering Levy’s past movies, we’re expecting an adventurous tone that blends well with Ghost Rider’s very striking, hellish visuals and darker themes.

Of course, this project is an invitation to add more magical beings to the MCU and explore the Strange-adjacent side of it. Maybe it’s our first step towards a Midnight Sons event movie? We can only hope.

Release date: December 15, 2028 | Director: Ryan Coogler | Cast: David Jonsson, Denzel Washington, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke

Ryan Coogler has taken a break from Marvel to make the excellent Sinners and help create a new iteration of The X-Files, but he’s confirmed to be coming back to wrap up his epic Black Panther trilogy. A while back, he confirmed he’d convinced Denzel Washington to join the MCU, and it sounds like those plans haven’t changed.

We also have a new T’Challa: David Jonsson (Alien: Romulus), who’s meant to play the son of the original T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman). If the years don’t make sense considering he was a kid in Wakanda Forever, wait until Secret Wars’ “soft reboot” for the answers.

What we know for sure is that series veterans Letitia Wright and Winston Duke are expected to stick around, but no plot details are available yet.

Release window: 2028 | Showrunner: Unconfirmed | Cast: Unconfirmed

Revealed at NYCC 2026, Zodiac is set to be Marvel Television’s next ongoing series after Daredevil: Born Again is over. Little is known about the premise at this point, though TV boss Brad Winderbaum has confirmed it’s a “globetrotting, international espionage show about secrets and lies and betrayals” with a packed cast of characters.

Word is the show is, more specifically, a British spy thriller with three leads, two male and one female. It’s expected to shoot in London during spring 2027, and chances are we’ll know much more about it well before that.

Of course, longtime Marvel TV fans are hoping for an Agents of SHIELD revival of sorts (its canonicity was never entirely clear), but it seems this show isn’t exactly that, though Clark Gregg (Agent Coulson) might be involved.

We’ve learned to never say never when it comes to Marvel comebacks, so stay tuned for more news.

Release windows: October 2027 / October 2028 / October 2029 | Showrunner: Bryan Andrews | Cast: Unconfirmed

Following a four-episode season in 2025, the animated series Marvel Zombies will be returning for three consecutive years (starting in 2027) just in time for Halloween.

The twist is that we’re now looking at three two-part specials: The Winter Soldier, The Fist of Khonshu, and The Last Guardian. It’s a huge departure from the previous plans with the Zombies and What If...? series, but it's one that could pay off.

Nothing is known about these small-scale projects at this point, but we know Marvel Zombies was a large enough hit on Disney+ to warrant more, and we’re okay with being surprised when it comes to format.

One has to assume these specials could work as one-shot comic books, but it’ll be interesting to see whether Marvel Television can tell cohesive and compelling stories with even shorter story arcs.

#553. ‘The Odyssey’ Takes Imax to Biggest Quarterly Revenue to Date

After a record-breaking summer season, Imax swung to its best-ever revenue and profits during the third quarter of 2026.

Fueled by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” the company’s highest grossing release of all time, Imax logged $175 million in revenue during Q3, up 64% from the $106.7 million reported in the same three-month period in 2025. Imax reported a net income of $117.1 million, a staggering 400% increase from the $22.6 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings-per-share rose to $2.21, up 370% from the 47 cents in the same year-ago period. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Animated Feature — A New and Competitive Era for the Medium That Isn't Just for Kids Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE)

As the industry enjoyed the biggest summer in post-pandemic times, Imax’s worldwide box office tally stood at $712 million, towering 94% above the $368 million posted a year ago. “The Odyssey” alone surpassed $550 million worldwide — representing 30% of the movie’s staggering $1.8 billion total haul. Those ticket sales crushed the company’s prior record-holder, 2009’s “Avatar,” with $271 million, not adjusted for inflation. “The Odyssey” was such a juggernaut on the company’s screens because it was the first feature shot entirely with Imax cameras. (Other tentpoles incorporate Imax’s technology for select sequences.) This quarter’s other top-earning titles were Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Resident Evil” and “Avengers Endgame Encore.”

“What Imax achieved goes beyond simply a ‘great quarter’ and transcends the many records we shattered in the period,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of Imax Corporation.” What we believe we are witnessing is an awakening to the power and potential of our platform to impact global culture, unlock new commercial opportunities, and inspire a new level of demand and awe in audiences around the world.”

Imax has been a true commercial draw in recent years, with audiences gravitating toward the big and bright screens to distinguish from the experience of watching a movie from the couch. Given the increased consumer demand, Imax continues to to expand its global footprint, signings agreements for over 100 systems worldwide to date in 2026 — 65% of which are for new locations. With blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday” (which is only playing in Imax in China) on schedule in December, Imax expects to exceed earlier projections of $1.4 billion in 2026. Last year, the company set a new record with $1.2 billion globally.

“We are excited for the year ahead and confident in our belief that there has never been a better time to be in the Imax business. This ‘Imax awakening’ sits inside a bigger culture shift of people around the world — particularly young people — seeking connection, community, and shared experiences that feel bigger than any one person’s screen,” Gelfond says. “Imax has always delivered these moments, and we believe this trend has only begun to benefit our business.”

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws.

"The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars, but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives.

"Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says.

Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity."

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization.

The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth. The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit.

Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030.

Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#551. Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation

Scientists have solved a biological mystery that remained unanswered for more than three decades, uncovering an unexpected way the immune system protects the body from its own inflammatory response. The breakthrough reveals that a chemical signal responsible for attracting immune cells to fight infections also helps prevent those same defenses from damaging healthy tissue.

The discovery came from researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), who took an unusual approach to studying inflammation. Rather than relying on mice, a standard choice for biomedical research, they turned to zebrafish. That decision helped them identify a long-mysterious enzyme and uncover a protective mechanism that had previously escaped scientists.

The findings, published October 7 in Nature, could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. They also raise the possibility of developing treatments that strengthen the body's natural defenses against inflammatory damage.

The mystery began in 1992, when researchers at McGill University investigated a molecule that helps direct immune cells toward sites of infection. Known as 5-oxoETE, or 5-oxo-6,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid, this fatty signaling molecule acts as a chemical alert when the body needs to respond to a threat.

At the time, scientists observed an enzyme that could both produce and break down 5-oxoETE. Enzymes are proteins that help chemical reactions take place, but in this case, researchers could not identify the human gene responsible for making the enzyme.

That missing genetic information created a major obstacle. Without knowing which gene produced the enzyme, scientists could not easily manipulate it in experiments or determine how problems with its activity might contribute to disease. Researchers assigned the enzyme a descriptive name based on its chemical function, but its genetic identity remained unknown for more than 30 years.

The breakthrough finally came through the work of Yanan Ma, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at MSK's Sloan Kettering Institute. Building on earlier investigations by former lab colleague King Lam Hui, PhD, Ma identified the human gene that produces the enzyme, giving researchers a way to examine its function much more closely.

How the Immune System Can Damage Healthy Cells

Ma works in the laboratory of cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD, whose research examines how cells respond to injuries, infections, and other forms of stress. His team focuses on inflammation, tissue repair, and regeneration, biological processes that also play important roles in cancer and numerous other diseases.

When harmful bacteria enter the body, chemical signals help recruit specialized white blood cells to the affected area. One of those signals is 5-oxoETE, which attracts immune cells equipped to attack invading microorganisms.

Although this response is essential for fighting infections, it carries risks. The substances immune cells release to destroy pathogens can also injure surrounding healthy tissue.

"They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control."

Niethammer's laboratory had already spent years investigating the molecular reactions involved in 5-oxoETE signaling. Researchers were gradually identifying how the different components of the system worked together, but the unknown enzyme remained a major missing piece.

Why Zebrafish Succeeded Where Mice Could Not

Most biomedical experiments involving animals use mice or rats because their biological systems share many similarities with humans. However, these familiar laboratory animals had a significant limitation for the question Ma and her colleagues wanted to answer.

"Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research," says Dr. Ma, who received a prestigious Marie-Josée Kravis WISE Fellowship in 2023 for her work on the pathway. "It makes sense -- they're mammals, and there's about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours."

Despite those similarities, mice lack a known immune cell receptor capable of recognizing 5-oxoETE. Without that receptor, researchers cannot investigate the complete signaling process in mice.

Zebrafish, however, have retained the necessary biological machinery.

"This means that you can't study the pathway in mice," Dr. Ma says. "But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds."

Using zebrafish allowed the scientists to explore how the signal operates in a living organism and eventually helped reveal a function that had gone unnoticed for decades.

Scientists Finally Identify the Missing Enzyme

Before investigating the process in zebrafish, Ma and Hui began searching for the enzyme's genetic origins using cultured human cells.

They selected several genes that might be responsible and systematically switched them off, looking for changes in the enzyme's activity. One candidate produced a decisive result.

When Ma disabled a gene called DHRS7, the enzyme stopped functioning. The experiment established that DHRS7 was the gene researchers had been searching for since the early 1990s.

Additional tests involving the rodent version of the gene showed almost no enzyme activity. That result was consistent with the absence of the 5-oxoETE receptor in mice, suggesting that rodents had lost key functions associated with this signaling system.

Identifying DHRS7 resolved the long-standing mystery. It also connected Ma's research with a separate investigation underway in the same laboratory, led by postdoctoral researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD.

"Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that's extremely important to note."

A Surprising Result Turns Expectations Upside Down

While Ma investigated the mysterious enzyme, Lengyel was using zebrafish to study colitis, an inflammatory condition affecting the colon. His experiments involved disabling selected genes to understand how they influenced intestinal inflammation.

One experiment produced an especially puzzling outcome.

Lengyel removed a gene called hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1). This gene produces the receptor that recognizes 5-oxoETE and allows cells to respond to its signal.

Because 5-oxoETE helps attract immune cells and initiate inflammation, removing its receptor should theoretically weaken that response.

"So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you'd expect less inflammation, not more," Dr. Lengyel says.

Instead, the zebrafish developed intestinal inflammation on their own, even though no infection was present.

The researchers initially considered whether neutrophils, the white blood cells normally recruited by the signal, might be responsible. However, removing those immune cells did not eliminate the inflammation.

This unexpected behavior suggested that the 5-oxoETE pathway was doing something much more complicated than simply activating the immune system.

Disabling an Inflammatory Signal Makes Inflammation Worse

The connection between the two research projects became clear after Ma identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme involved in 5-oxoETE signaling.

Lengyel then disabled DHRS7 in zebrafish, preventing the production of the enzyme and disrupting the signaling process.

Based on the molecule's established role in attracting immune cells, the researchers expected inflammation to decrease. Instead, they observed the same surprising pattern seen when the receptor was removed: inflammation increased.

"It made absolutely no sense," Dr. Lengyel says. "I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced."

The findings pointed to a previously unrecognized function. The signaling pathway did not simply help initiate the immune response. It also appeared to prevent unnecessary damage to healthy cells.

That dual responsibility explained why eliminating the pathway had such an unexpected effect. By disabling the system, scientists had removed not only an inflammatory signal but also an important source of cellular protection.

The Immune System's Hidden Protective Shield

Further experiments revealed how this protection works.

When immune cells attack dangerous microorganisms, they release highly reactive substances that can harm nearby healthy cells. The 5-oxoETE pathway helps tissues withstand this chemical stress, reducing the risk that the body's own defenses will cause unnecessary injury.

"This makes sense when you think about it," Dr. Niethammer says. "These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time."

The researchers found that zebrafish intestinal cells became particularly vulnerable when either 5-oxoETE or its Hcar1-4 receptor was missing. Even the normal bacteria living in the intestine produced enough low-level chemical stress to cause problems when this protective system was disabled.

The team traced the cellular protection to a group of enzymes known as NUDIX hydrolases. These enzymes help maintain cellular health by removing damaged DNA building blocks before they can interfere with normal biological processes.

Without the protective signaling pathway, intestinal cells could no longer withstand the chemical stress associated with ordinary gut bacteria. Some cells died, setting off an inflammatory response despite the absence of an invading pathogen.

The results revealed that the body uses the same molecular system both to call immune cells into action and to protect healthy tissue from the consequences.

"As it turns out, this signal isn't just an alarm, it's also a shield," Dr. Niethammer says.

Potential Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Diseases

Understanding this protective mechanism could have important implications for diseases involving excessive or poorly controlled inflammation.

The 5-oxoETE signaling pathway is known to be disrupted in conditions such as cancer, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and asthma. By identifying its previously unknown protective role, researchers have gained a new perspective on how those disruptions might contribute to tissue damage.

In human cancers, mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 (the human version of hcar1-4) have been identified in tumors of the gastrointestinal tract and uterus.

Research has also linked mutations that prevent OXER1 from functioning properly with poorer outcomes in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and kidney cancers.

The findings suggest that strengthening the pathway might eventually help healthy tissues tolerate damaging conditions more effectively. One possible application involves protecting the intestine from oxidative stress associated with cancer treatment.

"More research is needed, but there's a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress -- which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy," Dr. Lengyel says.

The discovery also has implications for diseases affecting mucosal tissues, the protective linings found in areas such as the intestines and respiratory tract.

In people with IBD, researchers have previously associated lower concentrations of 5-oxoETE in intestinal tissue with worse disease outcomes.

Evidence from asthma research points to another possible protective function. An independent study involving primates found that blocking OXER1 weakened the immune cell response but also caused protective mucus-producing cells in the airways to disappear.

Together, these observations suggest that attempts to suppress inflammation must account for the protective roles certain inflammatory signals perform. However, further research will be necessary to determine whether targeting this pathway can produce safe and effective treatments in humans.

How Physical Injury Activates the Same Defense System

The researchers are also investigating how this signaling pathway responds to physical damage, not just infection or chemical stress.

That aspect of the work is being explored by doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS, who studies how cells detect mechanical forces associated with tissue injury.

When cells experience physical stress, changes to their membranes can initiate the same chain of molecular reactions involved in inflammation.

One early step occurs when stressed cell membranes release arachidonic acid, a fatty molecule that serves as the starting material for producing 5-oxoETE.

Gelashvili, a co-author of the Nature study, led a separate investigation into the molecular signals associated with physical wounds. That research was published in Nature Communications earlier in 2026. His contributions were also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

"There's a mechanical component to the pathway that's upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying," explains Gelashvili, a co-author on the study who led a separate study on physical wound signals that was published in Nature Communications earlier this year; his work was also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences. "You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal."

The research suggests that the body combines information about different forms of cellular stress to coordinate its response. Physical damage can initiate the process, chemical stress can influence the conversion of signaling molecules, and DHRS7 helps strengthen the resulting signal.

Rather than operating as separate responses, these processes appear to work together to help the body recognize danger while limiting unnecessary harm to healthy cells.

"What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress -- mechanical and metabolic -- and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response," Dr. Niethammer says.

Additional researchers contributing to the study were Yohannes Ambaw, Leehyeon Kim, Ritchie Ly, Siyang Peng, Meysoon Quraishi, Tobias Walther, and Robert Farese Jr., all affiliated with MSK.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (R35GM140883); an MSK Basic Research Innovation Award; a Starr Foundation Program for Discovery Science grant; a Tow Foundation fellowship; a Marie-Josée Kravis Women in Science Endeavor (WISE) fellowship; a Crohn's Colitis Foundation Research Fellows Award (1268111); an Experimental Immuno-Oncology Scholars fellowship; and core facility services supported in part by MSK's National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant (P30CA008748).

After celebrating the victory, Kimmel turned to Trump and his claim that if he were on the ballot, the Republicans would have won more races. “That is such crap,” Kimmel responded. “You were on the ballot. You’re like dog hair; you’re on everything. You’ve infected every nook and cranny of our lives. You divided this country like no one else ever divided it before. The only time you ever brought us together was yesterday, when we all teamed up to get rid of you!”

Pointing out Trump’s own changes between political parties over the years, Kimmel said that he “has no allegiance to anyone or anything” and the “only party he leads is the slumber party.”

“The verdict is in, and there’s only one thing left for Nappy Gilmore to do: Resign,” Kimmel said. “Quit already, just quit. Nobody wants you. Even you don’t want to be president anymore. Take that billion dollars worth of crypto, buy an island. Maybe Epstein’s island? Wouldn’t that be a perfect end to this story!”

Kimmel then took the time to acknowledge a statement the White House put out about him in response to his monologue on the eve of the elections. “Jimmy Kimmel is a no-talent loser who has beclowned himself with tanking ratings and by spewing disgusting lies to his dwindling audience,” the statement from White House spokesperson Danny Ingle reads. “He is so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any commonsense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at him.”

Kimmel fired back: “Which is kind of the point of the show, but apparently I’ve beclowned myself once again. And that, by the way, almost word-for-word the same statement they’ve issued about me two times in the past year. I got a third beclowned, which I think is the last warning.”

But Kimmel delivered the ultimate zinger when referring to being called a “no-talent loser,” saying: “The last thing I want to do is tell you how to do your job, Danny Dingle, but today seems like a bad day for you to call me a loser.”

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan.

For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket. The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff.

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor.

The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one.

The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets.

The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission.

The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year.

The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads.

Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support.

In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice, a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response.

#548. Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

A new study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," said Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories

Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially important for maintaining healthy brain function.

During this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study shows that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep."

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans showed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age."

Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves."

The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

These observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

They collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon said.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain

Although memory often declines with age, the new research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

"It's not just about age," Sharon said. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate."

Sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide important indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

The findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

For now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

"We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon said. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions."

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT).

Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk. That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019.

Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off.

"The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3). That's a boost of about 30%.

Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

#546. Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation

Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."

#544. Stellantis stock rises 13% as automaker's turnaround plan, cost cuts gain traction

Shares of Stellantis were up Wednesday as the European car giant's third-quarter results showed it was making progress with its 60 billion euro turnaround plan.

Third-quarter revenues rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros from a year ago, the Chrysler and Jeep owner said on Wednesday, while adjusted operating income rose 184% to 256 million euros from 90 million euros a year earlier.

The automaker's industrial free cash flow improved to negative 4 billion euros, up from negative 4.3 billion the year prior.

Stellantis on Wednesday also reconfirmed its 2026 guidance and target to achieve positive free cash flow next year, which is a main focus for investors.

"Q3 was soft, but consensus expectations were far lower. Key here is that '26 Guidance was maintained while other auto OEMs and suppliers are cutting on elevated costs," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Wednesday in an investor note.

Stellantis stock on the New York Stock Exchange rose 13% on Wednesday to close at $4.69 a share. Shares in Milan closed at 4.28 euros, up 15.4%. Shares in both markets remain sharply down since the beginning of the year.

Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa told investors Wednesday that the company is ahead of schedule on its turnaround plan, which was announced in May. He said Stellantis expects to exceed its previously announced cost-cutting efforts of 6 billion euros under the plan by 2028, including 2.4 billion euros to start 2027.

"We are very confident in reaffirming our '26 guidance. Those include '27 free cash flow positive," Filosa said Wednesday in response to concerns about the carmaker's ability to achieve its free cash flow target.

Stellantis' 2026 guidance includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.

Stellantis' turnaround plan includes investing 36 billion euros in its portfolio of automotive brands, with 60% of the cash to go towards its struggling North America sector. It also plans to introduce new vehicles, refresh models, and incorporate new technologies in its products.

Stellantis is targeting roughly 23% revenue growth, from 154 billion euros last year to 190 billion euros by 2030, with a 7% adjusted operating margin by then.

European carmakers, including Stellantis, have been struggling in China as domestic brands like Xiaomi, BYD and Geely gain ground and intensify competition.

Just this week, German luxury carmaker Porsche said it would reduce its exposure to China as car sales decline in the region. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz said its third-quarter car sales slumped due to a "challenging market environment," in the country.

Earlier this month, Filosa told CNBC that European regulators need to do more to incentivize carmakers to manufacture vehicles in the region to fend off Chinese rivals.

Filosa called for regulation that "incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars."
